title: Medium Shot (MS)
narrative: Most scenes live in the medium shot because people talk with their hands. A glass, a phone, a cigarette, a slammed notebook all happen between waist and face.

Geography is still a little present (a booth, a window, a doorway) without becoming the subject. It is the wrong tool when the story is a walk, a costume from head to toe, or a face that must be the only landscape.
If you never leave this size, blocking becomes a radio play with heads and belts. Change size when the waist line no longer contains the fact.
how: Bottom frame at the waist or belt. Hands at rest should be in.
A 40mm to 50mm at conversational standing or sitting distance keeps perspective ordinary; the catalog 50mm is a default, not a law. Camera often at chest to eye height.
You should still read a bit of set, not a full room map. Prompt: Medium shot of [Subject] from the waist up, gesture and face in balance.
when: Use it as workhorse coverage: overlapping dialogue, a booth conversation, someone waiting with a suitcase handle in frame. Do not use it when the information is a holster below the hip, the feet, or a micro-expression that needs a closer crop.
vs: A Medium Close-Up starts at the chest and throws the waist away. A Cowboy Shot drops the bottom frame to mid-thigh so hands at the holster line stay in.
Medium is the waist sentence, not MCU and not cowboy. A Close-Up is a different sentence entirely: the face outranks gesture.
examples_film: His Girl Friday runs talk and gesture in this band so overlapping dialogue still has cigarettes, phones, and desks. Lost in Translation uses waist-up hotel and bar distance where two people can exist without becoming portraits or wide maps.
Grammar: conversation with hands.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Cowboy Shot (knees or mid-thigh in) or a Medium Close-Up (belt gone). The tell is either a gunbelt or a floating chest.
Fix: crop at the waist. Another tell is calling every talky frame a medium shot when it is an MCU.

faq.q: What is Medium Shot in film?
faq.a: A medium shot usually frames a person from the waist up so face and gesture share the frame. It is a size, sometimes called a waist shot, and it is the default band for a lot of scene coverage.

faq.q: Medium Shot vs Cowboy Shot
faq.a: A cowboy shot frames from mid-thigh or the knees up so hanging hands and a holster line remain. A medium shot cuts at the waist, so anything below the belt is out. If you can see thigh, you are not in a medium shot.

faq.q: When should I use Medium Shot?
faq.a: Use it when talk and hand business are the scene: tables, phones, glasses, notes. Do not use it when you need feet, a gunbelt, a full costume, or a face with no torso.

faq.q: How do I prompt Medium Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Medium shot of [Subject] from the waist up, conversational distance, 50mm. Keep hands in. Do not say cowboy, full body, or chest up.

title: Over-the-Shoulder Coverage (OTS)
narrative: OTS is default dialogue coverage with spatial glue. The partner remains physically present even in a close view.

Shoulder size and how much it obstructs can make the observer feel dominant, intimate, or trapped. It is the wrong tool when you need to isolate someone as if the other person had left the room: that is a clean single.
It is also the wrong tool if both faces are equally sharp and complete: that is a two-shot. An over-the-shoulder shot is a framing choice.
Shot/reverse shot is an editing pattern. They are not synonyms.
how: Place the camera beside one body, looking past a soft near shoulder at the far face. The far person looks at the near person, toward that shoulder, never into the lens.
Match foreground body position, head size, and eyeline on the reverse. The 180-degree line is the axis between the two bodies.
OTS coverage lives on one side of that line. If the near shoulder sits camera-right, the far face looks camera-right.

The reverse OTS swaps who is near, but it stays on the same side of the axis so screen direction does not flip. Crossing the line is not a style choice in this coverage: it makes two people look like they share a bench instead of a conversation.

Use focus and lighting to keep the speaking face sharp and the near cloth soft. Prompt: Over-the-shoulder framing of [Subject], near shoulder soft in foreground, the far face sharp, looking toward the near shoulder, 180-line held.

Never cross the 180-degree line. Draw the axis between the two people and keep the camera on one side of it. Far face looks at the near shoulder. The reverse stays on the same side of the axis. If they look into the lens or away from each other, it is no longer OTS coverage.
when: Use it as default dialogue coverage when you want the relationship to stay in the picture: a diner, a deposition, an interview through glass. Do not mismatch shoulder size on the reverse, and do not call a clean single an OTS.
vs: A Two-Shot gives both faces authorship. A Single removes the foreground partner; a dirty single may chew the edge without a true shoulder anchor.
A Reaction Shot may be taken as OTS or as a single. OTS means: near body fragment, far face subject.
Match the pair.
examples_film: The Social Network runs confrontations and depositions in this geometry. Heat 's diner uses shared geography and opposing coverage between the two-shot and the tighter work.

The Silence of the Lambs interviews live on whose shoulder, whose glass, whose face. The Stendhal Syndrome connects a person and a painting through alternating views, related grammar of looking past one thing at another.
Grammar: relation still in the foreground.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Two-Shot (both faces complete) or a Single (no shoulder). The tell is two people equally sharp, or a clean portrait.

The worse tell is a broken 180: the far person looks into the lens or away from the near shoulder, so the reverse would make them appear to sit on the same side. Fix: one soft shoulder, one sharp face looking at that shoulder, matched reverse, line held.

faq.q: What is Over-the-Shoulder Coverage in film?
faq.a: Over-the-shoulder coverage frames the far person as the subject while a near shoulder or head anchors the foreground. Paired OTS shots keep two people in a shared geometry even when we are close on one face.

faq.q: Over-the-Shoulder Coverage vs Single
faq.a: A single is one principal with no partner owning the foreground. OTS keeps a near shoulder or head in frame as a spatial glue. If the other person is gone from the rectangle, you have a single, even if they are still in the room.

faq.q: When should I use Over-the-Shoulder Coverage?
faq.a: Use it for dialogue that should keep the relationship physically present. Do not use it when isolation is the point, and do not mismatch the reverse.

faq.q: How do I prompt Over-the-Shoulder Coverage for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Over-the-shoulder framing of [Subject], near shoulder soft in foreground, the far face sharp, looking toward the near shoulder. Name who is near. Hold the 180. For video, generate a matched reverse as a second shot on the same side of the line, rather than spinning the camera around them.

faq.q: Does an over-the-shoulder shot break the 180-degree rule?
faq.a: No. A correct OTS is how you hold the 180. The camera stays on one side of the line between the two people. The far face looks toward the near shoulder, not into the lens. Crossing that line flips screen direction and is a coverage error, not a look.

title: Product
narrative: A product frame sells readability: logo plane, material, edges, how metal and glass behave. Speculars are designed, not accidental.
The background is often a sweep, a void, or a set built to disappear. It is the wrong tool when the object is a story fact inside a scene (a bloody letter on a kitchen table).
That is an insert, and it should keep the room's key. It is also the wrong tool if the camera orbits so fast the form never settles.
Show the object; let a Lazy Susan turn it if every side must read.
how: Choose a hero three-quarter or a true elevation. Large soft sources for wrapping highlights; flags and cards to kill ugly speculars on chrome.
Macro only for texture. A turntable or a slow orbit is a separate move.
Prompt: Product hero of [Subject], catalog clarity, controlled reflections, the object as the only subject.
when: Use it to sell the thing by lighting it like a face: a phone, a bottle, a watch on a sweep. Do not use drama-insert mess if you need catalog clarity, and do not use this glamour on a plot object that should look found.
vs: An Insert Shot lives in scene coverage as a plot fact, matching the room. Macro is an optic for small texture, which a product shot may use.
A Lazy Susan is a rotation method. Product is the commercial portrait job: controlled reflections, hero angle, the object as subject.
examples_film: Commercials and Apple keynotes are the public grammar: one object, clean plane, designed highlights, no accidental kitchen mess. Feature films sometimes steal this for a fetishized prop, which is a choice.
Grammar: catalog clarity, not found-object dirt, unless the brief is worn-in hero.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is an Insert Shot in dirty scene light, or a Macro texture with no hero angle. The tell is leftover room clutter, or a smear of uncontrolled speculars.
Fix: isolate the object, design the highlights, pick a hero angle.

faq.q: What is Product in film?
faq.a: Product cinematography frames and lights an object as the subject, with catalog clarity and controlled reflections, the way a portrait treats a face. It is a commercial or hero-object job, not a synonym for any close-up of a thing.

faq.q: Product vs Insert Shot
faq.a: An insert is a story detail inside a scene, usually matching that scene's light. A product shot isolates the object as a hero, often on a sweep or void, with designed speculars. A bloody envelope on a table is an insert; a phone on black acrylic is product.

faq.q: When should I use Product?
faq.a: Use it when the object must read as a designed hero. Do not use it for a plot fact that should stay in the room, and do not let reflections go unmanaged on chrome and glass.

faq.q: How do I prompt Product for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Product hero of [Subject], catalog clarity, controlled reflections, the object as the only subject. Name materials and background. For video, a slow turntable or a locked hero beat.

title: Reaction Shot
narrative: A reaction shot is coverage of receiving. The gunshot, the insult, the courtyard window: we often learn what it meant by looking at the person who saw it.
Meaning can be constructed between shots. A relatively still face reads differently depending on what came before, which is the Kuleshov lesson, not a demand that you fake a historical clip.

It is the wrong tool when the speaker's line still needs to be seen, or when you over-act the response so the audience is told the emotion. It is a function, not a size: often a close-up, sometimes an MCU, occasionally a full-body flinch.
how: Point the eyeline at the stimulus, even if that stimulus is offscreen. Hold.
Minimize explanatory mugging if you want the cut to do the work. Match Look Space and eyeline to the previous shot.
Size is usually Close-Up or Medium Close-Up . Prompt: Reaction close-up of [Subject] receiving news they cannot speak yet, the face as the cut.
when: Use it when the important action is watching: the face after an offscreen shot, the listener who cannot speak yet. Do not use it as a blink after every clause, and do not perform the entire emotion so the juxtaposition has nothing to do.
vs: A Close-Up is a size; a reaction is why that size is here. Over-the-shoulder coverage still includes the partner as a shoulder; a reaction single can drop them.
A Cutaway may be a non-human comment; a reaction is a person's response. Keep the face fixed if you want to test Kuleshov; changing the expression changes the experiment.
examples_film: The Godfather often lets receiving carry the beat. Whiplash cuts to the face that has to survive the next bar.
Rear Window builds Jeff's looks so courtyard views change what the same face means. Grammar: watch the watcher.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a generic Close-Up of the speaker, or an overplayed grimace. The tell is mouth moving through the line, or eyebrows explaining the plot.
Fix: this person is receiving, not delivering. Point the eyes; hold.

faq.q: What is Reaction Shot in film?
faq.a: A reaction shot shows a character's response to an event, a line, or an unseen stimulus. It is a coverage function: the important action is watching, and the face or body is what the cut is about.

faq.q: Reaction Shot vs Close-Up
faq.a: A close-up is a crop: head and upper shoulders. A reaction shot is a job: this image exists because of what was just seen or heard. Reactions are often close-ups, but a close-up of someone speaking is not a reaction.

faq.q: When should I use Reaction Shot?
faq.a: Use it when watching is the event and the audience should read the receiver. Do not stack one after every sentence, and do not over-act the face if the cut is supposed to supply meaning.

faq.q: How do I prompt Reaction Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Reaction close-up of [Subject] receiving news they cannot speak yet, the face as the cut. Put the eyeline in the prompt. Keep the expression restrained unless the scene needs a big flinch.

title: Single
narrative: A single isolates. The other person can still be in the room, but they no longer author the frame.
This is how you make someone alone during a conversation, or how you give a listener a private beat. It is not a oner and not a long take; those are duration.
A single is occupancy: one principal. It is the wrong tool when the relationship must stay visible as a shoulder or as a shared two-shot.
Going to singles too early turns every scene into ping-pong. Going to a clean single at the right time can feel like the partner has been erased.
how: Frame one person. For a clean single, keep edges empty of the partner ( Clean Frame ).

For a dirty single, allow a sliver of the other body as edge chew ( Dirty Frame ) without a composed foreground shoulder. Size is often Close-Up or Medium Close-Up , but a single can be a medium of one.
Prompt: Clean single of [Subject], one person, no foreground shoulder, the frame belonging entirely to them.
when: Use it to isolate: the other person is gone even if they are in the room. Do not leave a stray composed shoulder if you meant clean, and do not call a continuous long take a single just because one actor walks.
vs: Over-the-shoulder coverage uses the partner as a foreground anchor. A Two-Shot keeps both principals.
A Close-Up is a size a single often uses. A Oner is a long unbroken take, a different word.
Single means one occupant of the shot.
examples_film: The Silence of the Lambs uses clean, frontal singles in the interviews so the glass and the partner can vanish and the face owns the rectangle. That isolation is the coverage choice.
Grammar: one person, the rest of the relationship offscreen.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Over-the-Shoulder Coverage (composed near shoulder) or a Two-Shot . The tell is a sharp second face, or a textbook OTS.
Another tell is calling a oner a single. Fix: one principal, decide clean or dirty, do not confuse occupancy with duration.

faq.q: What is Single in film?
faq.a: A single is a shot containing one principal character. Clean singles keep other bodies out; dirty singles let a bit of the partner chew the edge. It is coverage occupancy, not a synonym for a one-take scene.

faq.q: Single vs Over-the-Shoulder Coverage
faq.a: OTS keeps a near shoulder or head as a compositional foreground while we watch the far face. A single removes that anchor so the frame belongs to one person. A dirty single is still a single; it is not a full OTS unless the near body is the viewpoint fragment.

faq.q: When should I use Single?
faq.a: Use it to isolate someone during or after a conversation. Do not jump there so early that the relationship never exists in frame, and do not confuse it with a oner.

faq.q: How do I prompt Single for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Clean single of [Subject], one person, no foreground shoulder. If you want dirty, specify a sliver of another body at the edge. Keep a second face out of the shot.

title: Three-Shot
narrative: A trio has politics. Two against one, a hinge person in the middle, a late arrival who splits a pair: the triangle is the story.

If you only cover this as ping-pong singles, the audience never sees who is left out in real space. It is the wrong tool when there are four or more as a unit, or when the scene has collapsed to a pair.
It is also the wrong tool if you line three heads up with equal light and equal height and call that drama. Someone should own a peak of the triangle, or stand in the cold of it.
how: Arrange three bodies as a triangle in depth or across the frame, not a flat police lineup unless the story is a firing squad. Triangular Composition helps, but blocking comes first: seats, levels, who faces whom.
Keep all three faces or postures readable enough to compare. Prompt: Three-shot of [Subject] in a triangular group, alliances and the odd one out readable in blocking.
when: Use it when a trio has politics: three gunmen, three people at a verdict, a couple plus the person who should not be there. Do not flatten them into equal portraits, and do not use a three-shot for a crowd.
vs: A Two-Shot is a pair; adding a third changes the grammar. A Group Shot holds a small ensemble larger than three as a relational unit.
A Master Shot may be a three-shot if the whole action is those three bodies. Do not treat three-shot as a synonym for any wide with extra extras.
examples_film: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly is the textbook trio: three men, three distances, one cemetery geometry. The standoff only works because all three remain comparable in shared frames before the eyes take over.
Grammar: three principals, readable alliance.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Two-Shot that crops the third, or a Group Shot with extras filling the sides. The tell is two faces and a shoulder, or a crowd.
Fix: three principals, triangular blocking, one of them slightly out.

faq.q: What is Three-Shot in film?
faq.a: A three-shot frames three principal people in one composition so their alliances, blocking, and who is left out are readable. It is not three close-ups in a row.

faq.q: Three-Shot vs Two-Shot
faq.a: A two-shot is a pair and the space between them. A three-shot adds a third principal and a triangle of politics. If the third person is only an out-of-focus extra, you still have a two-shot.

faq.q: When should I use Three-Shot?
faq.a: Use it when the scene's power is three-way: alliances, a hinge, an odd one out. Do not use it for a pair, and do not use it as a stand-in for a larger ensemble.

faq.q: How do I prompt Three-Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Three-shot of [Subject] in a triangular group, alliances and the odd one out readable in blocking. Name who is isolated. Keep all three readable.

title: Two-Shot
narrative: When the relationship is the shot, cutting to singles too soon steals the audience's ability to watch both people at once. A two-shot lets the viewer choose which face to read, and it makes a lean, a flinch, or a widening gap visible without an edit.
It is the wrong tool when one person must own the frame, or when a third body is politically in the scene. It is also the wrong tool as a timid wide that hides both performances.
Keep head sizes readable. Profile, 50-50, walking, or layered (one nearer) are variants of the same job: two people, one picture.
how: Balance or deliberately unbalance head sizes. Set a readable axis.
40mm to 50mm at table or walking distance is common. Decide whether one face is privileged by focus or light.
Small changes in distance are the acting. Prompt: Two-shot of [Subject] with a second figure, the space between them doing narrative work, 50mm, shared frame as relationship.
when: Use it when the relationship is the shot: two people at a diner table, a walk, a shared silence. Do not hide both faces in an unnecessarily empty wide, and do not use a two-shot if the scene has become a trio.
vs: Over-the-shoulder coverage puts one face in focus and the partner as a foreground shoulder; it is not a shared two-person portrait. A Single removes the partner.
A Three-Shot adds a third principal and a new politics. Two-shot means both people author the frame.
Shot/reverse is an editing pattern, not this size.
examples_film: Heat plants two opponents across one diner table before and between singles, so the gap is visible. Persona juxtaposes faces inside severe shared compositions.
Before Sunrise and The Apartment keep pairs in one frame so walking and apartment air are the relation. Grammar: two bodies, one sentence.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Over-the-Shoulder Coverage (one face plus a shoulder) or two singles cut together. The tell is one sharp face and a blur of coat, or both people so small the relation dies.
Fix: two principals, comparable scale, the gap visible.

faq.q: What is Two-Shot in film?
faq.a: A two-shot frames two principal subjects together so their relationship, distance, and posture are visible in one composition. The space between them is part of the shot, not only the faces.

faq.q: Two-Shot vs Over-the-Shoulder Coverage
faq.a: A two-shot gives both people authorship of the frame. Over-the-shoulder coverage uses a near shoulder as a foreground fragment while the far face is the subject. If you only see one face clearly, you are in OTS, not a two-shot.

faq.q: When should I use Two-Shot?
faq.a: Use it when the relationship is the event and the audience should watch both people at once. Do not use it as a timid wide that hides acting, and do not use it for a three-person politics problem.

faq.q: How do I prompt Two-Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Two-shot of [Subject] with a second figure, the space between them doing narrative work. Name whether they are in profile, facing, or layered. Keep both faces readable.

title: Video Portraits
narrative: A video portrait is not a close-up you cut away from after a line. You hold.
Blink, breath, a swallow, the tiny life in the face becomes the content. It sits closer to a painting that is allowed to live than to dialogue coverage .

It is the wrong tool when you need ping-pong coverage, a story insert, or a camera tour of the room. It is also the wrong tool if you freeze everything except one looping element: that is a cinemagraph.
Here the person is alive in small ways, and time is the point.
how: Lock the camera. Size a Close-Up or Medium Close-Up .
Light a simple, stable key. Hold long enough that duration registers (several seconds, sometimes much more).
No motivated move unless a tiny push is the brief. Prompt still: Video portrait of [Subject], a held face, duration as intimacy.
Motion brief: A long held portrait of [Subject], tiny life in the face, almost still.
when: Use it when a person is enough: a Screen Test, a study, an almost-still that breathes. Do not add a tour, and do not cut away the moment a thought appears; the hold is the piece.
vs: A Close-Up is a size used inside coverage; it usually leaves. A Cinemagraph freezes most of the image and loops one isolated motion.
A Single is occupancy of one body in scene coverage. A video portrait is duration plus stillness of a person as the entire event.
Interview testimony has a questioner; this may have none.
examples_film: Warhol's Screen Tests are the plain grammar: a person, a hold, time doing the work. The Irishman uses long, patient close-ups of faces that are allowed to sit, related in duration if not in art-historical setup.
Grammar: hold the person.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a dialogue Close-Up that wants a reverse, or a Cinemagraph with a frozen body and a looping steam jet. The tell is a camera move, a cut on a line, or a dead freeze.
Fix: lock off, keep the person slightly alive, hold.

faq.q: What is Video Portraits in film?
faq.a: A video portrait is a sustained study of one person at a stable size, with time itself as the intimacy. The face (or figure) is the whole event, almost still, with only tiny life in the features.

faq.q: Video Portraits vs Close-Up
faq.a: A close-up is a crop that often exists to deliver a line or a reaction, then leave. A video portrait uses a similar crop but stays: duration is the point. If you are about to cut to the other person, you are in coverage, not in a portrait study.

faq.q: When should I use Video Portraits?
faq.a: Use it when a person is enough and holding is the piece. Do not use it for ordinary shot/reverse, and do not turn it into a looping cinemagraph unless that is the brief.

faq.q: How do I prompt Video Portraits for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Video portrait of [Subject], a held face, duration as intimacy. For motion: A long held portrait of [Subject], tiny life in the face, almost still. Lock the camera. Allow only blink, breath, or a swallow.

title: Wide Shot (WS)
narrative: Size is a sentence. A wide shot maps who can reach the door, where the street goes, what weather is doing.
People are in the picture so we know the scale of the place, but the place is still talking. If you isolate too early, the scene loses its map.

It is the wrong tool when the beat is a face, a holster, or a head-to-toe costume portrait. It is also the wrong tool if the human has become an unreadable speck (extreme long shot) or if you only needed to declare the building before the scene (establishing as a job).
Use wide to keep geography in play, then change size when a new fact requires a tighter sentence.
how: Keep enough architecture, street, or weather that doors, paths, and weather remain readable. Bodies should not fill the height the way they do in a full-body portrait.

A 24mm in a room or a longer lens across a square can both be wide; the crop is whether place still speaks. Prompt: Wide shot of [Subject] in full environment, bodies small enough that place still speaks.
when: Use it when you must not isolate yet: who can reach the door, how far the platform runs, whether two groups can see each other. Do not crop into a full-body fashion frame and call it wide, and do not use it as a blank postcard with no relation to the scene's paths.
vs: A Full Body makes the complete figure the subject, head to toe, place as a border. A Long Shot is the person-in-world size: full figure plus geography, still a locatable human.
An Extreme Long Shot is speck-scale land. An Establishing Shot is a where-and-when job that often uses a wide.
A Master Shot is the action skeleton, which may be wide if blocking needs it. Wide is the environment-forward coverage attitude, not a synonym for those four.
examples_film: Once Upon a Time in the West lets station and desert speak while bodies remain small enough that place is the sentence. Lawrence of Arabia can sit in this band when geography is still coverage, not yet a speck-scale subject.
Grammar: keep the map; do not portrait.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Full Body (person fills the height) or a Long Shot labeled wide with no coverage job. The tell is a costume portrait, or a speck landscape with no scene paths.
Fix: place still speaks, bodies small enough to keep the map, geography that the next cut can use.

faq.q: What is Wide Shot in film?
faq.a: A wide shot shows the subject in a full environment, with bodies small enough that place still speaks. It is environment-forward coverage, not a synonym for full body, long shot, or establishing shot.

faq.q: Wide Shot vs Full Body
faq.a: Full body is a complete figure as the subject, head to toe, with environment as a readable border. A wide shot keeps place in charge: doors, streets, and weather remain the sentence, and people are small enough not to isolate yet. If the person fills the frame height, you are in full body, not wide.

faq.q: When should I use Wide Shot?
faq.a: Use it when geography must stay in play and you should not isolate yet. Do not use it as a head-to-toe portrait, and do not use it when scale should go to a speck.

faq.q: How do I prompt Wide Shot for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write Wide shot of [Subject] in full environment, bodies small enough that place still speaks. Name architecture and weather. Keep people from filling the height of the frame.

title: Animation
narrative: A drawing can hold a smear. A painted film can ignore a 180-degree shutter.
Spider-Verse can step the action and print halftone. Kaguya can let charcoal dissolve.
The 'camera' is a viewpoint in a constructed space. It is not Pixel Art (discrete sampling and a locked palette) and not Stop Motion (physical puppets moved a frame at a time).
Those are specific construction methods. Animation as a look means designed light and graphic motion, in 2D, 3D, or hybrid.
how: Decide the construction: 2D volumes, CG with graphic shaders, or mixed. Light is keyed in the design, not motivated only by a set practical unless you invent one.
Motion: smears, holds, stepped frame rates, or full 24fps. Do not default to photoreal ray-traced blur unless that is the film.
Prompt graphic volume, designed light, motion as drawing rather than photography.
when: Use it when the world must be constructed, not captured. Do not use it as a filter on live action that still wants real lens physics, and do not collapse it into pixel tiles or puppet stop-motion unless that is the method.
vs: Animation is constructed motion and light. Pixel Art is tiled, paletted sampling.
Stop Motion is physical increment. Video Game is playable camera logic (follow cam, HUD, collision), which may be animated or live-action dressed as a game.
A photoreal CG shot that imitates a 50mm still is animation as production, not this graphic look.
examples_film: Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse (stepped motion, graphic halftone, designed light). The Tale of the Princess Kaguya (charcoal and watercolor as cinematography).
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is photoreal live action, Pixel Art , or Stop Motion . The tell is a 50mm bokeh plate, chunky sprites, or puppet seams you did not want.
Fix: specify the graphic medium, design the key as paint or shader, and choose smear or stepped motion.

faq.q: What is Animation in film?
faq.a: A constructed look: light and motion are designed (drawn, painted, or shaded), not captured through a lens, unless you deliberately simulate a lens. Graphic volume replaces photographic exposure.

faq.q: Animation vs Pixel Art
faq.a: Pixel art locks sampling and palette into visible tiles. Animation may be fluid charcoal, cel, or graphic 3D. Both are constructed. Only pixel art makes the pixel the unit of the world.

faq.q: When should I use Animation?
faq.a: When the world cannot or should not be a photographed place. Skip it if you want a real lens, if you want visible tiles, or if you want puppet stop-motion specifically.

faq.q: How do I prompt Animation for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Animated treatment of [Subject], graphic volume, designed light, motion as drawing rather than photography. Name charcoal, cel, or halftone. Do not request photoreal bokeh by default.

title: Arthouse
narrative: Someone sits. The room keeps being a room.
Headroom is a little wrong. The light is a window, not a rim.
You are allowed to get bored, which is how thought enters. Negative space is not a mistake.
It is the wrong tool when the shot must play on a billboard or when the camera should hunt. Blockbuster Gloss shapes every edge.
French New Wave is impatient and jump-cut. Photography may also hold still, but as a print: posed, decisive, often centered.
Arthouse can be off-center, slightly ugly, and long.
how: Lock the tripod. 35mm or 50mm spherical, modest stop, available or window key, little or no fill.
Allow odd headroom and Negative Space . Do not add a backlight rim unless the room has one.
Color stays mixed or quietly naturalistic. Prompt patience, odd headroom, natural light, the frame willing to be empty, duration implied.
when: Use it when a beat needs time and air more than emphasis. Do not use it on an action geography pass, and do not confuse it with a centered stills-like tableau.
vs: Arthouse is empty, patient, and often slightly mis-framed. Blockbuster Gloss is the opposite finish.
Negative Space is a composition tool. Static Locked-Off is the locked camera.
Photography pretends to be a print: posed light, decisive moment. Arthouse may refuse the decisive moment and keep running.
examples_film: Toni Erdmann (plain light, social duration, frames that do not flatter). Roma (65mm black-and-white patience, even when the set is full).
Drive My Car (holds on cars, rooms, and grief). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Blockbuster Gloss or Photography : a rim-lit poster, or a perfectly posed print. The tell is a hair light, centered beauty, and no empty duration.
Fix: lock off, raise the headroom, kill the rim, and let the room stay a room.

faq.q: What is Arthouse in film?
faq.a: A patient look: locked camera, odd headroom, natural light, and a willingness to be empty. The frame leaves time for thought instead of selling a poster.

faq.q: Arthouse vs Blockbuster Gloss
faq.a: Arthouse withholds polish and fills the frame with air. Blockbuster gloss rims, contrasts, and designs the sky so the still could sell tickets. Choose based on whether emptiness is allowed.

faq.q: When should I use Arthouse?
faq.a: When a scene needs space and duration more than emphasis. Skip it for action posters, for vérité hunting zooms, or for a posed photographic tableau that wants to be a print.

faq.q: How do I prompt Arthouse for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Arthouse still of [Subject], patience, odd headroom, natural light, the frame willing to be empty, static camera. Name the unused air. Do not add a heroic rim.

title: Blockbuster Gloss
narrative: Adventure as a still that could sell the film. Faces are shaped.
Horizons are clean. Dust and haze exist to carry god-rays, not to hide information.
39 anamorphic, but the finish is expensive contrast, not empty duration. It is the wrong tool when thought needs space or when cheapness is the truth.
Arthouse leaves headroom and waits. Stylistic Suck would be dishonest here in reverse: polish is the contract.
Teal and Orange is a grade you can apply to anything. Gloss is the whole package: rim, scale, cleanliness.
how: Key plus a strong backlight rim. Add haze for Volumetric Light shafts.
Keep skies clean or dramatically designed, not stained by accident. 24mm to 40mm for scale, longer glass for faces if the format is large.
Grade: expensive contrast, often teal-orange, highlights rolled but still bright. Prompt expensive contrast, clean skies, heroic rim, IMAX-scale finish, adventure poster in motion.
when: Use it when the shot must play on a billboard and the world should look funded. Do not use it for a quiet empty interior, a vérité interview, or a decaying porch.
vs: Blockbuster Gloss is rim, scale, and clean contrast. Teal and Orange is only the grade.
Volumetric Light is only the shaft. Arthouse is the opposite contract: patience and empty frame.
Maximalism packs pattern. Gloss can be relatively simple, just expensive.
Dystopian dirties the civic future. Gloss polishes the adventure.
examples_film: Mad Max: Fury Road (hard sun, rims, desert contrast built for large screens). Dune (2021) (volumetric shafts, monumental wides, controlled haze).
Skyfall (poster-clear action geography, expensive night and landscape). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Arthouse emptiness or a Teal and Orange grade on a poorly lit face. The tell is no rim, stained accidental skies, and a frame that would not read as a poster.
Fix: add a backlight rim, clean the sky, and raise the contrast until the silhouette holds at small size.

faq.q: What is Blockbuster Gloss in film?
faq.a: A large-scale adventure finish: high contrast, clean or designed weather, a heroic rim, volumetric shafts, and billboard-readable geography. The image is built to sell and to parse far from the screen.

faq.q: Blockbuster Gloss vs Arthouse
faq.a: Gloss fills and shapes: rim, contrast, poster horizon. Arthouse leaves space, odd headroom, and duration. One is afraid of emptiness. The other uses emptiness as the point.

faq.q: When should I use Blockbuster Gloss?
faq.a: When the beat must read as a funded adventure still. Skip it for vérité, for decaying humidity, for empty arthouse holds, or for a teal-orange grade with no rim and no geography.

faq.q: How do I prompt Blockbuster Gloss for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Blockbuster gloss on [Subject], expensive contrast, clean skies, heroic rim, volumetric haze, IMAX-scale finish. Name the horizon. Do not ask for odd headroom or unstyled mixed color.

title: BTS
narrative: The shot admits the apparatus. An actor holds a mark.
A boom dips. The apartment has no fourth wall.
You came for the scene and got the factory that makes it. That leak can be comic, tender, or cruel.
It is not Cinéma Vérité of real life, and not a sit-down Interview unless you plant one on the set. It is documentary rhetoric aimed at a film set.
Documentary of a non-film subject will not show stands and flags.
how: Two lighting worlds: the scene's motivated key on the actor, and unstyled worklight on crew and the studio. Include a stand, a flag, a slate, or the unfinished set edge.
Camera: observational handheld or a wider locked shot that keeps crew readable. Do not pretty the crew with the movie rim.
Prompt crew, stands, and the set edge visible, the fiction leaking, documentary light on a constructed world.
when: Use it when the making must be visible, not only the make-believe. Do not use it as a vérité street look with no set, and do not hide every stand if you claimed BTS.
vs: BTS is a set with its crew visible. Cinéma Vérité is real life with a filmmaker.
Documentary is evidence rhetoric at large. Interview may appear inside BTS (a director talk) but is not the leak of the set.
If there is no apparatus in frame, it is not behind the scenes.
examples_film: Day for Night (a production as the subject, the set as a factory). Living in Oblivion (independent-set chaos as comedy).
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Cinéma Vérité or a clean production still: street vérité, or the scene with no crew. The tell is a finished fourth wall and no stands.
Fix: show the wall missing, a flag, a person with a boom, and mixed worklight.

faq.q: What is BTS in film?
faq.a: Behind-the-scenes coverage: crew, stands, and the unfinished set visible in the same frame as the fiction. Documentary light on a constructed world, so the making leaks.

faq.q: BTS vs Cinéma Vérité
faq.a: Vérité watches unstaged life. BTS watches a set. Both may be handheld and mixed-color. Only BTS needs C-stands, flags, and a missing fourth wall as the subject.

faq.q: When should I use BTS?
faq.a: When the story or the still must show the making. Skip it for recovered-tape horror, for street vérité with no set, or for a finished scene with the apparatus hidden.

faq.q: How do I prompt BTS for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Behind-the-scenes look at [Subject], crew, C-stands, and the set edge visible, worklight mixed with the scene key. Name a flag or boom. Do not hide the apparatus.

title: Cinéma Vérité
narrative: Life is not staged for a key light. Someone talks, the zoom finds them, a window or a practical is the source, and the filmmaker's question or proximity changes what happens.
The frame can be late, centered wrong, or blown at the window. That is the contract.
It is the wrong tool when polish is the point, or when a fictional camcorder is the story. Blockbuster Gloss would be propaganda here.
Found footage needs a diegetic operator in danger. Documentary is broader: interviews, archive, and observation that may sit back.
how: Available light only, or a small on-camera bounce that still reads as room light. 16mm or a long ENG zoom (the 12-120 class), hunting focus and size.
Handheld or a monopod, eye height, reacting. Leave mixed tungsten and daylight.
Do not add a rim or a pretty backlight. Prompt available light, unpretty frames, zooming to find, life unstaged.
when: Use it when style would feel like a lie and the filmmaker's presence is part of the event. Do not use it as a shake filter on a scripted scene that still has three-point lighting.
vs: Cinéma vérité is intervention and available light in documentary reality. Documentary includes sit-down interviews and archive.
French New Wave borrows the tools for fiction, then adds jump cuts and cinephile blocking. Handheld is only the body.
Available Light is only the source. Found Footage invents a tape inside the story.
examples_film: Don't Look Back (zoom-to-find, dressing rooms, a public figure not styled for film). Primary (campaign interiors, available light, the camera in the room).
The Battle of Algiers (newsreel immediacy as a staged cousin of this grammar). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Found Footage or pretty Documentary : a timestamp and panic, or a keyed interview with a clean backlight. The tell is three-point light, a rim, or a device story.
Fix: kill the film lights, let the zoom hunt, and keep the filmmaker in the room as a presence, not a horror operator.

faq.q: What is Cinéma Vérité in film?
faq.a: A documentary look in which available light, zoom-to-find framing, and the filmmaker's presence provoke or witness unstaged life. The camera is a catalyst, not a hidden observer with a key and a rim.

faq.q: Cinéma Vérité vs Documentary
faq.a: Documentary is a broad rhetoric: interview, archive, observation, even mock forms. Cinéma vérité is a specific physical method: available light, zoom, presence. A sit-down with a window key can be documentary without being vérité.

faq.q: When should I use Cinéma Vérité?
faq.a: When prettifying the room would feel like propaganda, and the filmmaker's being there matters. Skip it for recovered-tape horror, for billboard gloss, or for a scripted scene that still wants a rim light.

faq.q: How do I prompt Cinéma Vérité for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Cinéma vérité treatment of [Subject], available light, unpretty frames, zooming to find, mixed color, life unstaged. Name the real source. Do not add a timestamp, a rim, or a crane.

title: Cosmic Horror
narrative: The frame makes the person a mistake. A horizon does not match.
A structure has too many vanishing points. Light may be too hard, too colored, or too revealing, so looking is the harm.
Underlighting turns a familiar face into a specimen. It is the wrong tool for a slasher in a cabin or for family rot on a porch.
Giallo is a gloved human. Southern Gothic is kin and heat.
Cosmic horror needs the universe, a lab, an ice, a shimmer, or a ship that is also a geometry error.
how: Start too wide: Extreme Long Shot of land, ice, or a structure that is the wrong size. Cheat perspective (forced, dutch, non-matching vanishing points) a little, not as cartoon expressionism.
Light faces from below or from a source that has no sun logic. Overexpose the revelation.
Palette: Antarctic bounce, alien shimmer, or red that is not a gel gag. Prompt scale wrong, geometry slightly illegal, a brightness that reveals too much, human irrelevance.
when: Use it when the threat cannot be a person and the image must make knowledge dangerous. Do not use it for a masked killer in a hallway, or for a foggy swamp that is still a family story.
vs: Cosmic horror is scale, illegal geometry, and revealing light. Extreme Long Shot is only size.
Underlighting is only the angle. German Expressionism bends sets as a mind; cosmic horror bends them as an alien fact.
Southern Gothic keeps humans too near. Dreamcore is a soft liminal room, not a cosmos.
examples_film: The Thing (1982): Antarctic bounce, isolation wides, a body that will not stay a body. Annihilation : shimmer, wrong color in daylight, landscape as mutation.
Event Horizon : a ship interior whose lighting and geometry refuse comfort. Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a slasher, Southern Gothic , or generic fog. The tell is a human antagonist filling the frame, or a porch.
Fix: widen until the person is small, break one vanishing point, and let the source be too bright or from below.

faq.q: What is Cosmic Horror in film?
faq.a: A look that makes humans optically irrelevant: wrong scale, slightly illegal geometry, under-light or over-revealing brightness, and a threat that is not a person. Knowledge is the harm.

faq.q: Cosmic Horror vs Southern Gothic
faq.a: Southern gothic traps you in kin, heat, and a house. Cosmic horror traps you in a universe that will not parse. One is too close. The other is too large and too wrong.

faq.q: When should I use Cosmic Horror?
faq.a: When the antagonist cannot be a man and looking is dangerous. Skip it for slashers, for family decay, for giallo gloves, or for a foggy swamp with a human in it.

faq.q: How do I prompt Cosmic Horror for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Cosmic horror framing of [Subject], scale wrong, geometry slightly illegal, a brightness that reveals too much, human irrelevance. Name the horizon error. Do not ask for a masked killer.

title: Documentary
narrative: The camera claims evidence. A sit-down by a window.
A wide of work being done. A cutaway that pretends to prove the sentence.
Comedy and unease both live in the gap between what people say and what the camera appears to witness. It is broader than Cinéma Vérité .
Vérité hunts with a zoom and admits the filmmaker as catalyst. Documentary may also plant a stable interview, use archive, or build a fictional crew ( Interview style, observational B-roll).
It is not Found Footage : there is usually an implied production, not a lost tape.
how: Leave mixed color. Window key for interviews, 35mm to 50mm, eye level, interviewer often offscreen.
Observational wides on a zoom, focus hunting is allowed if the implied crew would hunt. No hair light unless the real room has one.
Imperfect coverage only when it fits that production. Prompt mixed color, unstyled wardrobe light, zoom finding focus, respect without glamour.
when: Use it when pretty would be a lie, or when a fiction wants interview-versus-observation irony. Do not use it as random shake, and do not swap it for a recovered-camera story.
vs: Documentary is a rhetoric (interview, observation, archive). Cinéma Vérité is a method (available light, presence, zoom-to-find).
Found Footage is a diegetic recorder. Available Light is the source only.
BTS shows a film set's crew. Mockumentary uses documentary rhetoric on invented people.
Quality check: those are not interchangeable.
examples_film: The Act of Killing (reenactment and interview as evidence). Honeyland (observational patience, mixed natural light).
Won't You Be My Neighbor? (archive plus sit-down).
This Is Spinal Tap and Best in Show (fictional crews using interview and observation). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Found Footage or glossy interview: a horror camcorder, or a keyed talk show. The tell is a timestamp, or a Hollywood hair light on a 'documentary' subject.
Fix: pick a crew style, mix the color, and let the zoom or the window be the only flattery.

faq.q: What is Documentary in film?
faq.a: A look and a rhetoric: observational wides, sit-down interviews, archive, mixed color, and unstyled light. Fiction can wear the same clothes (mockumentary) without becoming found footage.

faq.q: Documentary vs Cinéma Vérité
faq.a: Vérité is one documentary method: presence, available light, zoom-to-find. Documentary as a look also includes stable interviews and archive. A window-keyed sit-down can be documentary and still not be vérité.

faq.q: When should I use Documentary?
faq.a: When the image must look like evidence, or when a fiction needs the gap between testimony and observation. Skip it for recovered-tape horror, for vérité-only catalysis, or for glamour rims.

faq.q: How do I prompt Documentary for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Documentary look on [Subject], mixed color, unstyled wardrobe light, zoom finding focus, interview or observational coverage. Name the crew position. Do not add a camcorder timestamp or a hair light.

title: Dreamcore
narrative: A corridor continues too far. A fluorescent is a little green.
A window is over-bloomed like a memory. The person may be small or absent.
Nothing jumps. The dread is that the room will not resolve into a place you can leave.
It is not Weirdcore (low-res digital, captions, early-web jokes that threaten). It is not Altered State (smear, afterimage, unhooked color as perception failure).
It is not Magical Realism (a recognizable world with one impossible fact treated as weather). Dreamcore is the memory-room.
how: Wide 24mm to 35mm, eye level, often locked. Soft sources: fluorescent, a cheap tungsten lamp, a blown window.
Keep contrast low. Fog the blacks a little.
Palette: 1990s suburban pastel or pool cyan, slightly sick. Empty the mid-ground.
Prompt liminal rooms, soft dread, childhood lighting gone wrong, a memory that will not resolve.
when: Use it when nostalgia must lose its safety in an empty interior. Do not use it for JPEG horror, for a miracle in daylight realism, or for a warped trip sequence.
vs: Dreamcore is soft analog liminal space. Weirdcore is degraded digital and captioned.
Altered State warps the image physically. Magical Realism keeps ordinary light and one impossible fact.
If you add clipart and 240p, you have left dreamcore.
examples_film: Synecdoche, New York (rooms that replicate and will not end, theater as a memory warehouse). The Backrooms culture (liminal empty interiors as internet folklore).
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Weirdcore or Altered State : chunky artifacts and captions, or trailing edges. The tell is low-res clipart or a trip warp.
Fix: keep resolution continuous, soften the key, empty the corridor, and let the light be almost-childhood.

faq.q: What is Dreamcore in film?
faq.a: A liminal, soft-interior look: empty rooms, childhood practicals gone wrong, low contrast, and unresolved space. Nostalgia remains. Safety does not.

faq.q: Dreamcore vs Weirdcore
faq.a: Dreamcore is analog-soft and spatial. Weirdcore is early-web: low-res, cropped, captioned, a joke that threatens. One is a room you almost remember. The other is a file you should not have opened.

faq.q: When should I use Dreamcore?
faq.a: When an empty interior must feel like a memory with the safety removed. Skip it for captioned JPEG horror, for perception smear, or for a daylight miracle in a real town.

faq.q: How do I prompt Dreamcore for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Dreamcore image of [Subject], liminal rooms, soft dread, childhood lighting gone wrong, low contrast, empty hall. Do not add captions, JPEG crunch, or trip smear.

title: Dystopian
narrative: A checkpoint. A tower.
A crowd compressed by a long lens, or a handheld walk through trash and concrete. The sky is rarely clean.
The person is ranked by clothing, by queue, by a logo on a wall. It is not automatically Tech Noir .
Tech noir is wet guilty night and investigation, screens as keys. Dystopia can be a grey afternoon, a refugee camp, an orange industrial fog, with no detective.
Bleach Bypass can drain the silver. It is a process, not the whole civic design.
how: Two common modes: dirty handheld 35mm with available mixed light and lens dirt (civic collapse), or monumental wides with haze, fog, and controlled orange or grey (state scale). Keep surfaces used: stains, signage, rank.
Avoid heroic rims unless the regime would light itself that way. Prompt civic scale gone cold, haze, signage, and rank, a future that already feels used.
when: Use it when the system, not a single villain, has to be visible in the streets. Do not use it as generic grey sci-fi, or as neon crime with no civic rank.
vs: Dystopian is used civic future. Tech Noir is noir crime inside a machine night.
Bleach Bypass is a desaturated silver process. Blockbuster Gloss polishes adventure.
If the city is wet, neon, and investigative, check whether you actually want tech noir. If the sky is clean and rim-lit, you have left dystopia.
examples_film: Children of Men (handheld civic dirt, 35mm, long-take streets, a used near-future). Blade Runner 2049 (monumental fog, orange, rank, and scale).
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Tech Noir or Blockbuster Gloss : neon rain investigation, or a poster-clean future. The tell is a hard noir cheek with no civic rank, or a rim-lit sky.
Fix: dirty the surfaces, add signage and haze, and decide handheld-civic versus monumental-fog.

faq.q: What is Dystopian in film?
faq.a: A look in which civic scale, used surfaces, haze, signage, and rank make the system the antagonist. The future already looks worn. Daylight bureaucracy counts as much as night rain.

faq.q: Dystopian vs Tech Noir
faq.a: Tech noir is crime grammar plus future screens at night. Dystopian is the used state: queues, towers, pollution, rank, often in day. Overlap exists. They are not the same lighting plot.

faq.q: When should I use Dystopian?
faq.a: When the system must be visible as the threat. Skip it for silver 1940s crime, for pastel vaporwave, for glossy adventure, or for a neon detective story with no civic rank.

faq.q: How do I prompt Dystopian for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Dystopian view of [Subject], civic scale gone cold, haze, signage, and rank, used surfaces. Name the queue or tower. Do not default to neon detective rain.

title: Film Noir
narrative: The shot withholds the room. A face is half a mask.
Guilt has to live in the sliver that remains, which is why voice-over can sit on this image without explaining the picture. Streets are wet so the night has a specular path back to the lens.
It is the wrong tool when the crime is colorful, fashionable, or futuristic. If the threat is a gelled primary, use Giallo .
If the night is neon and the year is now, use Neo-Noir . If the architecture itself is bent, use German Expressionism , not a wet street.
how: Key with a hard Fresnel or open-face through slats, 45 to 90 degrees off camera, fill killed so the ratio sits near 8:1. Wet-down the street so the same key returns as bounce.
Practicals (desk lamp, cafe sign, streetlamp) must match the direction even if they are not the exposure. Lens: 35mm for a street, 50mm for a face, moderate stop so walls fall off.
Camera locked or a short dolly, eye level or a touch below. Prompt the gobo, the unfilled cheek, the wet asphalt, and 1940s crime blocking.
when: Use it when a character steps under a streetlamp and the shadow has to accuse them. Do not use it as a generic dark-crime grade on a color-saturated fashion interior.
vs: Film noir is silver, hard, and unfilled. Neo-noir keeps the guilty geometry but paints it with color practicals.
Tech noir adds future screens as keys. Giallo is the opposite palette: hyper-saturated primaries, not black-and-white pools.
German Expressionism distorts the set; noir usually keeps real streets and lets light do the distortion. Kit cousins: Low-Key Lighting , Gobo Lighting , Wet-Down , Chiaroscuro .
examples_film: The Third Man (wet Vienna, hard raking keys, a face in a doorway). Double Indemnity (venetian gobos, a confession in a dark living room).
The Big Combo (a fogged spotlight as the only map of a killing ground). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Neo-Noir or generic Low-Key Lighting : color neon rain, or a softly underexposed room with no hard edge. The tell is a filled shadow, dry pavement, and no slat texture on the wall.
Fix: kill the fill, add a venetian or tree cookie, wet the ground, and keep the palette silver.

faq.q: What is Film Noir in film?
faq.a: A 1940s crime look built from hard, unfilled keys, gobo texture, wet streets, and eye-level 35mm or 50mm blocking. The picture withholds information. Silver contrast does the work that color would do in later noir.

faq.q: Film Noir vs Neo-Noir
faq.a: Film noir is low-key silver with tungsten practicals and wet-down bounce. Neo-noir keeps the guilty geometry but keys with color: sodium, neon, and contemporary flesh. If you can name a gel hue as the mood, you have left classic noir.

faq.q: When should I use Film Noir?
faq.a: When a crime scene needs the room to refuse the face: a doorway, a slatted office, a wet alley. Skip it for fashion-horror color, future screens, or any beat that needs a readable, filled close-up.

faq.q: How do I prompt Film Noir for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Film-noir treatment of [Subject], hard venetian gobos, unfilled far cheek, wet-down street, 50mm spherical, 1940s crime blocking. Specify the practical that motivates the key. Do not ask for color neon or a soft underexposed room.

title: Found Footage
narrative: Knowledge is limited to what the operator can point at. What the camera misses is part of the beat.
Autofocus hunts a doorway. A timestamp sits in the corner.
The person holding the camera is in danger too, which is why the frame is late, dirty, and incomplete. Handheld footage alone is not found footage.
If there is no fictional origin for the tape, you have Handheld or stylistic suck . If a documentary crew is interviewing, you have documentary rhetoric, not a recovered camcorder.
how: Choose the device: Hi8, MiniDV, early digital, or a phone. Match its wide-ish zoom, auto exposure pumping, rolling shutter, and focus hunt.
Keep a plausible operator position and a reason the camera stays on. Night-vision is a mode of that device, not a grade.

Do not add a crane or a pretty close-up the operator could not have taken. Prompt consumer digital or Hi8, timestamp, autofocus hunt, amateur framing, and documentary panic as the operator's, not the film's.
when: Use it when the operator is inside the event and the tape could later be found. Do not use shake as the entire premise, and do not use it for an omniscient amateur look with no diegetic camera.
vs: Found footage needs a diegetic recorder. Handheld is a body-mounted tool in an otherwise omniscient film.
Stylistic Suck can look cheap without a recovered-tape story. Cinéma vérité puts a filmmaker in real life as a catalyst, not a character's camcorder.
Night Vision is one mode the found camera may switch into. Documentary uses interview and observation, not a lost tape.
examples_film: The Blair Witch Project (recordings presented as the missing filmmakers' tapes). REC (a television crew's camera as the constrained record).
Cloverfield (a personal camcorder framing a disaster). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Handheld shake or Stylistic Suck ugliness with no operator. The tell is a perfect close-up, a crane, or coverage the character could not have shot.
Fix: pick the device, keep one operator position, let focus hunt, and let the frame miss the action.

faq.q: What is Found Footage in film?
faq.a: A narrative that presents images as recordings made by someone inside the fictional events, often discovered afterward. The camera's limits (timestamp, battery, autofocus, amateur framing) are the grammar.

faq.q: Found Footage vs Handheld
faq.a: Handheld is how the camera is held. Found footage is who owns the tape. You can have a stable found camera (a shelf cam, a news rig). Shake without a diegetic recorder is not found footage.

faq.q: When should I use Found Footage?
faq.a: When the operator is in the scene and the story depends on what that device can and cannot see. Skip it for omniscient cheapness, for sit-down interviews, or for any shot the character could not have taken.

faq.q: How do I prompt Found Footage for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Found-footage camera on [Subject], consumer digital or Hi8, timestamp, autofocus hunt, amateur framing. Name the operator and why the camera stays on. Do not request a second angle or a crane.

title: French New Wave
narrative: Youth and impatience with studio polish. A character talks to the lens.
A walk is a burst of handheld, then a jump cut skips the boring meters. Paris oxygen, or any city's equivalent, is the lighting plot: windows, cafes, overcast streets.
It is not cinéma vérité . Vérité is documentary presence.

New Wave is authored fiction using documentary tools plus cinephile grammar ( Jump Cut , freeze, iris, a look at the camera). It is also not found footage: there is no recovered tape, only a director in the street.
how: Location interiors, available or small practicals, 35mm or 50mm on a Cameflex-class body, handheld or a light tripod. Shoot the walk, then jump-cut in the edit.
Reflexive beats: eyeline to camera, a sudden insert. Street daylight, cafe tungsten, no matching backlight.
Prompt jump cuts implied, street light, jump-into-life framing, handheld Paris oxygen as location air, not as a mood word.
when: Use it when a young, restless fiction needs streets, jump cuts, and impatience with coverage. Do not use it for studio three-point polish or for a camcorder-horror premise.
vs: French New Wave is fiction plus location plus Jump Cut . Cinéma Vérité is documentary catalysis.
Handheld is the body only. Documentary may interview.
New Wave characters still act a story. Arthouse may be slower, emptier, and less cinephile-playful.
The New Wave camera is in a hurry.
examples_film: Breathless (jump cuts on the street and in the room, a look to camera). The 400 Blows (location childhood, available light, a final run).
Cléo from 5 to 7 (real-time Paris, streets and interiors as a clock). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Cinéma Vérité or Found Footage : a documentary claim, or a tape. The tell is a news timestamp, a horror shake, or glossy three-point.
Fix: keep it fiction, keep it location, handheld or light tripod, and let the edit jump.

faq.q: What is French New Wave in film?
faq.a: A fiction look from late-1950s France and its heirs: location shooting, street and practical light, handheld cameras, jump cuts, and reflexive cinephile grammar. Studio polish is the enemy.

faq.q: French New Wave vs Cinéma Vérité
faq.a: Vérité documents real people and lets the filmmaker provoke. New Wave stages a story with the same cameras and streets, then jump-cuts and looks back at the lens. One is documentary method. The other is fiction with documentary tools.

faq.q: When should I use French New Wave?
faq.a: When a restless fiction belongs on a sidewalk or in a cheap apartment, and coverage would feel like a studio. Skip it for recovered-tape horror, for vérité documentary, or for billboard gloss.

faq.q: How do I prompt French New Wave for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: French New Wave energy on [Subject], location street light, handheld 35mm, jump cuts implied, jump-into-life framing. Name the cafe or sidewalk. Do not add studio rims or a camcorder timestamp.

title: German Expressionism
narrative: Psychology is built, not implied. A staircase leans.
A shadow is bigger than the body that casts it, and sometimes the shadow is paint. The face is lit like a mask because the room is already a diagnosis.
It is the wrong tool for a real wet street or a fashion interior. Noir keeps plausible cities and lets Hard Light do the violence.
Giallo bends color, not carpentry. If the walls are square and only the grade is moody, you do not have expressionism.
how: Build or paint impossible architecture: converging walls, oversized windows, stairs that refuse the horizon. Light with hard, unfilled sources so shadows are graphic edges, not soft falloff.
Dutch the camera a few degrees as a default, not a sting. Orthochromatic or high-contrast black-and-white, 35mm spherical, theatrical blocking, often locked-off.
Prompt painted shadows, impossible architecture, jagged light, and Caligari psychology as set.
when: Use it when the location must be a mental state, not a real address. Do not use it as a dutch-angle garnish on a square contemporary room.
vs: German Expressionism distorts carpentry. Film Noir distorts with light on real streets.
Dutch Angle is one tilted horizon; expressionism is the whole set. Hard Light is the source quality.
Chiaroscuro is the ratio. You need the bent architecture, not only the contrast.
examples_film: The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (painted shadows, canted town as a mind).
Metropolis (shafts, scale, and machine geometry as social diagram). Nosferatu (a body that is also a shadow on a wall).
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Film Noir or a lone Dutch Angle : a wet alley, or a tilted camera in an ordinary room. The tell is square architecture with only contrast added.
Fix: cant the set or the perspective, paint or project graphic shadows, and lock the camera on that geometry.

faq.q: What is German Expressionism in film?
faq.a: A look in which distorted sets, painted or graphic shadows, hard unfilled light, and stylized blocking make the location a psychological diagram rather than a real street.

faq.q: German Expressionism vs Film Noir
faq.a: Noir keeps plausible cities and cuts them with gobos. Expressionism rebuilds the city as a bent mind. Both love hard light. Only one makes the staircase illegal.

faq.q: When should I use German Expressionism?
faq.a: When a character's inner state has to be walked through as architecture. Skip it for crime on real wet streets, for gelled fashion-horror, or for a dutch angle with nothing else changed.

faq.q: How do I prompt German Expressionism for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: German expressionist treatment of [Subject], painted shadows, impossible architecture, jagged hard light, dutch horizon. Specify the illegal wall or stair. Do not prompt a normal room plus contrast.

title: Giallo
narrative: Horror here is also wardrobe. A cobalt window, a red hallway, black leather in the foreground.
The frame is chic until the glove enters. Subjective threat is a color, a zoom, and a Dutch Angle , not a wet black alley.
It is the wrong tool for low-key crime or for density-as-ornament. Film Noir withholds with black.
Maximalism fills every zone with pattern for pleasure. Giallo uses primaries as a weapon inside relatively designed, often sparse, interiors.
how: Gel the keys: red, green, cobalt through windows or colored glass, so the palette is primary, not pastel. Keep contrast high but chroma higher.
35 Techniscope wides for interiors. Dutch a few degrees on the kill or the stare.
Foreground a black glove, a blade, or a fashion object. Prompt hyper-saturated primaries, implied black leather, Argento color crime, and beauty as the lighting on the face, not a slogan.
when: Use it when a stylish interior has to turn hostile through color, a zoom, and a gloved hand. Do not use it as generic saturated horror or as noir with a red grade.
vs: Giallo is gelled primaries and fashion-threat. Film Noir is unfilled silver.
Hyper-Saturation is a grade; giallo is that grade plus zoom, dutch, and leather-glove blocking. Maximalism packs ornament; giallo often leaves chic negative space and stains it with one violent hue.
Dutch Angle is a tilt. Giallo uses the tilt as one tool among gels and zooms.
examples_film: Suspiria (1977): colored glass as motivated key, dance-school architecture as a trap. Deep Red : zoomed inserts, primary interiors, investigation as fashion-horror.
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Film Noir or plain Hyper-Saturation : a fedora night, or a loud grade with no glove, no gelled window, and no zoom. The tell is teal-orange rain or even, pretty color with no threat axis.
Fix: pick one primary as the key, dutch or zoom toward the threat, and put a dark fashion object in the foreground.

faq.q: What is Giallo in film?
faq.a: An Italian mystery-horror look: gelled primary color, fashion interiors, zooms, dutch angles, and stylized violence. The lighting is often glamorous. The threat arrives as a color and a glove.

faq.q: Giallo vs Film Noir
faq.a: Noir withholds with black and wet silver streets. Giallo attacks with red, green, and cobalt in designed interiors. Both can dutch the camera. Only giallo treats a window gel as the murder weapon.

faq.q: When should I use Giallo?
faq.a: When horror has to look like a fashion spread until the glove enters. Skip it for silver crime, for future neon investigation, or for busy ornament that is not a threat.

faq.q: How do I prompt Giallo for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Giallo look on [Subject], hyper-saturated primaries, gelled window key, black leather in the foreground, 35mm zoom implied. Name the primary. Do not ask for noir silver or a generic saturated grade.

title: Magical Realism
narrative: A girl sees a monster and the exposure does not change. Snow falls in a kitchen and the practicals stay kitchen practicals.
Wonder is not a lighting cue. If you add shafts, dutch angles, and a choir of haze, you have left the contract.
It is not Dreamcore (liminal rooms, unresolved memory). It is not Altered State (perception smear).
It is not blockbuster spectacle. The world stays real.
One fact does not.
how: Motivated naturalistic light: window, overcast, a household bulb. 35mm or 50mm, eye level, coverage as if nothing were impossible.
Play the miracle in the same size you would play a kettle. Do not under-light, dutch, or add volumetric spectacle for the impossible beat.
Prompt ordinary light, one impossible fact treated as weather.
when: Use it when a miracle must not become a set-piece. Do not use it for a trip sequence, a liminal corridor, or an effects showcase.
vs: Magical Realism keeps ordinary light and one impossible fact. Dreamcore empties and softens the room.
Altered State warps perception. Southern Gothic can host strange events but its optical problem is heat and decay, not a calmly covered miracle.
If the camera gawks, it is spectacle, not this look.
examples_film: The Spirit of the Beehive (honeyed natural light, a child's encounter played as afternoon). Beasts of the Southern Wild (aural and visual wonders inside humid daylight realism).
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Dreamcore , Altered State , or gloss: a liminal hall, a smear, or a volumetric miracle. The tell is a lighting change at the impossible beat.
Fix: keep the same key, the same lens height, and stage the impossibility as weather.

faq.q: What is Magical Realism in film?
faq.a: A look that covers extraordinary events with ordinary, motivated light and realist blocking. The camera does not change grammar for the miracle. The world stays recognizable. One fact does not.

faq.q: Magical Realism vs Dreamcore
faq.a: Dreamcore is an unresolved liminal interior with childhood light gone wrong. Magical realism is a real town or house with one impossible fact played like weather. Different rooms, different contracts.

faq.q: When should I use Magical Realism?
faq.a: When a miracle must not become spectacle. Skip it for trip warps, for empty memory halls, for cosmic scale, or for a lighting cue that announces wonder.

faq.q: How do I prompt Magical Realism for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Magical-realist image of [Subject], ordinary light, one impossible fact treated as weather, 35mm eye level, no extra rim. Name the room and the single impossibility.

title: Maximalism
narrative: Wallpaper fights the costume. A pastry fights the uniform.
Pink fights purple. The eye has no rest unless a centered axis organizes the noise (a hotel lobby) or a smash of hue refuses rest (a dance hall).
Speed and scale can join the density, but the optical fact is abundance. It is not Giallo .
Giallo stains relatively chic space with a weaponized primary. Maximalism fills the space with pattern for its own sake.
Hyper-Saturation is a grade. You can saturate a empty desert and still not be maximalist.
how: Short to moderate lenses (24mm to 40mm) to pack furniture and pattern. Multiple colored practicals.
High chroma, high detail, often symmetry or a center line so the density composes. Keep enough stop that wallpaper does not melt into bokeh unless a close-up needs it.
Prompt too much color, too much pattern, density as the point.
when: Use it when a world is ornamental, theatrical, or stuffed, and a sparse frame would deny that world. Do not use it as a loud grade on an empty room, or as giallo threat with one gel.
vs: Maximalism is packed production design plus chroma. Giallo is fashion-threat primaries.
Hyper-Saturation is the grade only. Blockbuster Gloss can be relatively clean and expensive.
Arthouse empties. If you can count three competing patterns and they are all in focus, you are in maximalism.
examples_film: The Grand Budapest Hotel (centered density, uniforms, pastry, wallpaper as architecture). Moulin Rouge !
(theatrical color, patterned interiors, speed as ornament). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Giallo or Hyper-Saturation : one violent gel, or a loud grade on bare walls. The tell is empty negative space and a single hue.
Fix: fill every zone with pattern, keep it sharp, and let several colors compete.

faq.q: What is Maximalism in film?
faq.a: A dense look: ornament, pattern, and chroma packed into every zone, with light that keeps the clutter readable. Abundance is the optical fact, not a side effect.

faq.q: Maximalism vs Giallo
faq.a: Giallo uses primaries as threat inside often chic, relatively sparse interiors. Maximalism fills the interior with pattern for pleasure or theatrical excess. Both can be saturated. Only one is a murder-fashion plot.

faq.q: When should I use Maximalism?
faq.a: When restraint would lie about the world: a hotel, a stage, a stuffed apartment. Skip it for empty arthouse air, for noir silver, or for a single gelled hallway.

faq.q: How do I prompt Maximalism for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Maximalist frame of [Subject], too much color, too much pattern, density as the point, multiple practicals, clutter sharp. Name the wallpaper. Do not empty the frame.

title: Neo-Noir
narrative: The city is still a trap, but the trap has a hue. Rain carries magenta and cyan.
A sodium streetlamp turns a raincoat mustard. The moral geometry (half a face, a wet street, a figure stranded in a pool of light) survives.
Only the stock is color. It is the wrong tool when you need period silver, future screens as the only keys, or candy primaries as threat.
Classic Film Noir has no neon to name. Tech Noir puts crime inside a digital city.
Vaporwave uses pink-cyan without guilt or investigation.
how: Keep a hard key 45 to 90 degrees off, but let practical color do the fill: neon in rain, sodium overhead, a tungsten interior leaking onto wet asphalt. Contrast stays high.
Skin may go teal-shadow, orange-highlight, or stay mixed on purpose. Lens: 35mm or 40mm anamorphic, or spherical 35mm, often at night with rain as the volume.
Camera: locked wides, slow tracking, occasional push-in on a face. Prompt color where classic noir was silver, name the neon practicals, and keep the rain.
when: Use it when a present-day or period-color crime scene needs melancholy and rain, not a 1940s silver print. Do not use it as a teal-and-orange grade on a scene with no hard key and no guilty blocking.
vs: Neo-Noir is color noir: same isolation, new practicals. Film Noir is the silver original.
Tech Noir adds science-fiction production design and screens as sources. Teal and Orange is a grade, not a genre look; you can grade a comedy teal-orange and still have no noir blocking.
Neon Practicals is the lamp. Neo-noir is the lamp plus the crime geometry.
examples_film: Chinatown (period color, hard sun and venetian interiors, investigation as a trap). Blade Runner (rain, smoke, neon as key, still a detective picture).
Drive (night exteriors, pink-cyan practicals, locked-off melancholy). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Film Noir (you asked for color and got a black-and-white fedora) or a Teal and Orange grade with no key. The tell is a filled, even night or a palette with no motivated practical.
Fix: add a named neon or sodium source, keep the hard ratio, and wet the ground.

faq.q: What is Neo-Noir in film?
faq.a: Noir themes and blocking restaged after color: hard keys, rain, isolation, and crime, lit by sodium, neon, and tungsten instead of silver nitrate night.

faq.q: Neo-Noir vs Film Noir
faq.a: Film noir withholds with black-and-white contrast and tungsten gobos. Neo-noir withholds with color practicals. Same guilty geometry, different stock. If the frame has no hue you can name, it is not neo-noir.

faq.q: When should I use Neo-Noir?
faq.a: When a color crime scene needs rain, neon, and a face half in shadow. Skip it for 1940s silver, for future-corporate screens ( Tech Noir ), or for pastel mall nostalgia ( Vaporwave ).

faq.q: How do I prompt Neo-Noir for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Neo-noir look on [Subject], color where classic noir was silver, neon practicals, rain, hard key, unfilled cheek, contemporary crime blocking. Name cyan or magenta signage. Do not stop at a teal-orange slider.

title: Photography
narrative: Hold. This is the picture.
A candlelit room is arranged like a painting. A river still is exposed for the sky.
People occupy the frame as if a shutter, not a scene, were about to close. It is close to Arthouse patience but not the same.
Arthouse may be empty, slightly ugly, and long. Photography wants the print: a chosen moment, shaped light, a composition that would survive without time.
If the camera hunts, you have left the still.
how: Tripod. One frame.
Pose the bodies or wait for a still gesture. Light as a stills photographer would: window, candle, or a single shaped key, not a moving TV-style fill.
35mm to 85mm, sometimes a zoom used as a stills crop (as in Barry Lyndon ). Prompt still-photography grammar, a single decisive frame, posed light, the movie pretending to be a print.
when: Use it when the beat is a picture, not a passage. Do not use it for coverage that must cut, or for empty duration that refuses to compose.
vs: Photography is the print as grammar. Tableau is staged group composition.
Centered Composition is a placement rule. Arthouse may refuse the decisive moment.
Static Locked-Off is only the locked head. A photographically lit moving shot can still be this look if every frame could hang.
A locked empty hold with odd headroom is arthouse first.
examples_film: Barry Lyndon (candlelit stills, zoom as a painter's crop). The New World (natural light, frames that behave like exposed plates).
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Arthouse emptiness or a moving coverage scene: odd unused air, or a walk-and-talk. The tell is a frame that would not survive as a still, or a camera that hunts.
Fix: lock, compose as a print, and shape one light.

faq.q: What is Photography in film?
faq.a: A look that treats motion pictures as prints: decisive framing, posed or found stills light, often tableau or centered, with the camera behaving like a shutter rather than like coverage.

faq.q: Photography vs Arthouse
faq.a: Both may lock the camera. Arthouse uses duration and empty air, even if the still is imperfect. Photography wants a picture that could hang: posed light, a chosen moment. One waits. The other composes.

faq.q: When should I use Photography?
