faq.a: When the beat is a still: a portrait, a landscape plate, a candlelit tableau. Skip it for hunting vérité, for jump-cut streets, or for empty holds that refuse to compose.

faq.q: How do I prompt Photography for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Still-photography grammar on [Subject], a single decisive frame, posed light, tripod, the movie pretending to be a print. Name the print type. Do not add a hunting camera.

title: Pixel Art
narrative: The world is tiles. If the beat is actually Video Game , change the setup instead of forcing pixel art.
how: For pixel art: a genre look is light, palette, lens, and blocking together, not the genre name alone. In a prompt it reads like this: Pixel-art treatment of the subject, chunky samples, limited palette, game-sprite cinema.
Write a start state, one change, and an end frame the next shot can inherit.
when: The world is tiles. Do not use pixel art to make a frame look expensive.
Prefer Video Game when that cousin's job is the one you actually need.
vs: Pixel Art is easy to confuse with Video Game , Animation . Stay on pixel art when the world is tiles.
If the beat is Video Game , shoot that instead.
examples_film: Pixel Art is easier to picture if you remember " Wreck-It Ralph adjacent ", " indie games ". Borrow camera, light, and subject relationships, not a copyrighted still.
mistakes: The usual failure is asking for pixel art and getting Video Game . Pixel Art is easy to confuse with Video Game , Animation .
Stay on pixel art when the world is tiles. If the beat is Video Game , shoot that instead.

faq.q: What is pixel art in film?
faq.a: Pixel art builds the image from visible tiles or a low-resolution grid. The world is discrete squares, not continuous grain. The world is tiles.

faq.q: Pixel Art vs Video Game: what is the difference?
faq.a: Pixel Art is easy to confuse with Video Game , Animation . Stay on pixel art when the world is tiles. If the beat is Video Game , shoot that instead.

faq.q: When should I use pixel art?
faq.a: The world is tiles. Do not use pixel art to make a frame look expensive. Prefer Video Game when that cousin's job is the one you actually need.

faq.q: How do I prompt pixel art for AI image or video?
faq.a: Lead with who does what. Camera, light, and style follow. Do not replace physics with mood adjectives. Still clause: Pixel-art treatment of the subject, chunky samples, limited palette, game-sprite cinema. At most one motivated camera move per clip. The last frame is law for the next shot.

title: Southern Gothic
narrative: Beauty is rotting. A house peels.
Sweat holds on skin. Sun through moss becomes a moving gobo.
The palette is gold-green and tobacco, not cyan neon. Blocking is slow: a porch, a church, a river, a dinner table that will not end.
It is the wrong tool for urban night crime or for cosmic scale. Film Noir is a wet city.
Cosmic horror makes the human irrelevant against illegal geometry. Southern gothic keeps the human too close: kin, pulpit, swamp.
how: Late sun as key, often raking, through trees or moss so the pattern crawls. Add atmospheric haze or real humidity so blacks go milky.
Porch bulbs and interior practicals go warm and a little dirty. 35mm or 50mm spherical, sometimes 24mm for a house against sky.
Avoid clean rims. Let paint peel in the highlight.
Prompt humid decay, moss, late-afternoon gold gone sickly, beauty rotting as production design, not as a slogan.
when: Use it when heat, family, and decay have to be visible in the air. Do not use it as generic gothic fog on a Victorian stone castle, or as noir in a Southern town with the humidity removed.
vs: Southern Gothic is humid gold-green decay. Dappled Light is the moss gobo only.
Atmospheric Haze is the air only. Cosmic Horror is scale and illegal geometry.
Film Noir is urban night silver. A British gothic look is stone, grey, and cold.
Keep the heat.
examples_film: The Night of the Hunter (river, moonlight, and a Southern fable's hard shadows). Beasts of the Southern Wild (humid daylight, water, a community at the edge of weather).
True Detective S1 (sickly gold, industrial coast, family rot). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Film Noir or generic gothic fog: wet city silver, or a cold castle. The tell is no humidity, no moss pattern, and a teal night grade.
Fix: add late sickly sun, haze, peeling surfaces, and slow porch blocking.

faq.q: What is Southern Gothic in film?
faq.a: A look that makes the American South's heat, decay, and haunted social history optical: sickly gold, moss dapples, humidity, porch practicals, and slow blocking around family and land.

faq.q: Southern Gothic vs Cosmic Horror
faq.a: Southern gothic keeps human kin too close: a porch, a pulpit, a swamp. Cosmic horror shrinks the human against wrong scale and geometry. One is family rot. The other is the universe refusing you.

faq.q: When should I use Southern Gothic?
faq.a: When heat, family, and something under the porch must be visible. Skip it for urban noir, for future rain, or for a cold stone gothic with no humidity.

faq.q: How do I prompt Southern Gothic for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Southern gothic air around [Subject], humid decay, moss, late-afternoon gold gone sickly, porch tungsten, peeling paint. Name the house and the heat. Do not ask for a wet city or a cosmic void.

title: Spaghetti Western
narrative: Myth is dirt, sweat, and a horizon that refuses shade. The sun is a weapon.
A Cowboy Shot shows the holster. An Extreme Close-Up of the eyes shows the decision.
The land is wide. The soul is a few millimeters of iris.
It is the wrong tool for a clean studio western or a misted martial landscape. American A-westerns often fill the faces and keep the sky polite.
Wuxia uses silk, mist, and wire, not ochre and hard noon.
how: 35 spherical. Pair a 24mm or 28mm for the town and ridge with a 75mm to 135mm (historically much longer) for the eye.
Hard sun as key, little or no fill, dust as diffusion. Grade: burnt umber, bleached sky, dry highlights.
Blocking: hip-level cowboy size for guns, then the operatic hold on the face. Prompt Techniscope grit, dusty ochre, extreme close-ups of eyes, sun as a weapon.
when: Use it when a standoff needs dirt, a hard sun, and a cut from landscape to iris. Do not use it for a polished sunset ride or for martial-arts mist.
vs: Spaghetti Western is hard sun, ochre, Techniscope, and eye ECUs. Cowboy Shot is only the size (mid-thigh).
Extreme Close-Up is only the size of the eye. Hard Light is the source.
The look is those tools in a dusty, morally dirty western, not a filled Hollywood campfire. Wuxia is the cousin in landscape myth with the opposite weather.
examples_film: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (plaza wides against eye close-ups, bleached sun). Once Upon a Time in the West (operatic holds, Harmonica's face as a landscape).
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a glossy adventure western or Wuxia : rim-lit horses, polite skies, or bamboo mist. The tell is filled faces, teal-orange grade, and no eye ECU.
Fix: kill the fill, bleach the sky, add dust, and jump from a wide plaza to the eyes.

faq.q: What is Spaghetti Western in film?
faq.a: A western look built in Italy and Spain: Techniscope wides, hard sun, ochre dust, cowboy-size gun coverage, and telephoto eyes. The rhythm is operatic. The morals are dirty.

faq.q: Spaghetti Western vs Wuxia
faq.a: Both use landscape as myth. Spaghetti western is dry, hard, and ochre, with eye close-ups. Wuxia is mist, silk, and wire-assisted paths. Different weather, different lens pair.

faq.q: When should I use Spaghetti Western?
faq.a: When a standoff or a ridge arrival needs dirt and an unfilled sun. Skip it for martial mist, for IMAX-clean adventure gloss, or for night neon crime.

faq.q: How do I prompt Spaghetti Western for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Spaghetti-western frame of [Subject], Techniscope grit, dusty ochre, hard sun, no fill, extreme close-up of eyes, cowboy-shot holster. Do not ask for a clean sunset poster.

title: Stylistic Suck
narrative: Auto-exposure pumps. A zoom overshoots a face.
Fluorescent kitchens go green. Highlights blow like 1990s VHS.
The film is allowed to look poorly made because that look is the argument: poverty, joke, cruelty, or anti-beauty. It overlaps Found Footage but is not the same.
Found footage needs a diegetic operator and a tape story. Stylistic suck can be omniscient and still ugly: no timestamp required.
It also overlaps Cinéma Vérité , but vérité hunts in order to witness. Suck hunts in order to fail, as style.
how: Consumer camcorder or VHS: auto gain, hunting zoom, rolling shutter, blown practicals, wrong WB left wrong. Allow bad centering.
Do not 'fix' in the grade. If you add a pretty close-up, you have broken the contract.
Prompt deliberate amateur look, bad zoom, cheap video, the wrong white balance as a choice.
when: Use it when polish would be dishonest. Do not use it as accidental incompetence, and do not use it as found footage without an operator story.
vs: Stylistic Suck is the film choosing ugliness. Found Footage is a character's recorder.
Cinéma Vérité is available-light witnessing. Documentary may still be respectful and sharp.
If there is a timestamp and a diegetic reason the camera exists, you are in found footage. If the ugliness is the film's voice, you are here.
examples_film: The Blair Witch Project (amateur optics; also found footage, so use it as overlap, not as the whole definition). Trash Humpers (VHS, blown highlights, ugliness as the work).
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Found Footage : you add a timestamp and an operator without meaning to. The tell is a recovered-tape premise you did not want, or a pretty backup angle.
Fix: keep the film's camera ugly and omniscient, or commit fully to a diegetic device if that is the story.

faq.q: What is Stylistic Suck in film?
faq.a: A chosen amateur look: hunting zooms, cheap video, wrong white balance, blown highlights. The film's own camera refuses polish. It does not require a recovered-tape story.

faq.q: Stylistic Suck vs Found Footage
faq.a: Found footage needs a diegetic recorder and a reason the tape exists. Stylistic suck can be the movie looking poorly made with no operator character. Blair Witch is both. Trash Humpers is suck as voice.

faq.q: When should I use Stylistic Suck?
faq.a: When polish would lie. Skip it if you need a recovered-camera plot, if you need vérité respect, or if a single pretty angle would sneak back in.

faq.q: How do I prompt Stylistic Suck for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Deliberate amateur look on [Subject], bad zoom, cheap video, wrong white balance as a choice, blown practicals. Do not add a timestamp unless the camera is also a story object.

title: Tech Noir
narrative: The future is wet and guilty. A detective, a fugitive, or a machine walks rain that is lit by advertisements and monitors.
The face is still half in shadow. The key is no longer only a streetlamp.
It is a billboard, a terminal, a police scanner. It is not all dystopia and not all neo-noir.
Dystopian can be daylight bureaucracy and civic scale with no crime plot. Neo-Noir can be a present-day parking garage with sodium lamps and no future tech.
Tech noir needs both the investigation geometry and the machine city.
how: Keep noir ratios: hard key, unfilled cheek, wet ground. Replace tungsten with screens and LEDs as motivated keys, plus residual sodium or neon.
Smoke or rain for volume. 35mm or 40mm anamorphic, night exteriors, occasional long-lens compression of towers.
Blocking: figures small under signage, then a close-up keyed by a display. Prompt future crime, screens as practicals, rain, corporate night, analog noir in a digital city.
when: Use it when a future city is also a crime scene and the screens light the guilt. Do not use it for a clean utopian interface, or for present-day noir with no speculative design.
vs: Tech Noir is noir plus science-fiction sources. Neo-Noir is color noir without requiring future tech.
Dystopian is the used civic system, often in daylight, with the state as antagonist. Neon Practicals is the lamp.
Film Noir is the silver ancestor. If there is no screen, tower, or machine as light, you are still in neo-noir.
examples_film: Blade Runner (rain, neon, and a detective plot inside a machine city). The Terminator (1984 night, tech-noir club and streets, analog crime against a future machine).
Ghost in the Shell (1995) (screens, rain, and investigation as identity). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Neo-Noir or generic Dystopian : contemporary neon crime, or a grey megacity with no investigation geometry. The tell is no screen as a source, or daylight civic haze with no wet guilty night.
Fix: add a display key, rain, towers, and a crime blocking of isolation.

faq.q: What is Tech Noir in film?
faq.a: A fusion of noir lighting and crime structure with science-fiction design. Screens and corporate night become the practicals. Rain stays. Guilt stays. The city is digital. The grammar is still investigation.

faq.q: Tech Noir vs Neo-Noir
faq.a: Neo-noir is color noir in a later or present world. Tech noir requires speculative technology as light and as threat. Blade Runner is both. A 2010s parking-garage crime film may be neo-noir only.

faq.q: When should I use Tech Noir?
faq.a: When the future is a wet crime scene and a screen lights the face. Skip it for silver 1940s noir, for daylight civic dystopia, or for pastel vaporwave with no investigation.

faq.q: How do I prompt Tech Noir for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Tech-noir on [Subject], future crime, screens as practicals, rain, corporate night, hard unfilled key. Name the display. Do not stop at neon rain with no speculative city.

title: Vaporwave
narrative: Nostalgia for a catalog that closed. A bust, a grid floor, Japanese retail signage, a sunset that is a gradient more than a sun.
Highlights bloom like consumer tape. The mood is mall-at-closing, not investigation.
It is easy to confuse with Neo-Noir because both like cyan and magenta. Noir still wants a hard key, rain guilt, and a face in shadow.
Vaporwave wants even pastel fill, sculpture, and tape artifacts. Cross Process can supply the hue shift.
It is not the whole look.
how: Soft, even sources: fluorescent mall, plus a pink or cyan gel as a wash, not a hard key. Center the subject.
35mm spherical, moderate depth. Add VHS: chroma bleed, slight tracking error, soft resolution.
Set dressing: marble, palms, Greek busts, grid, sunset gradient. Prompt pink-cyan gradient, marble and palms, VHS bleed, mall-at-closing melancholy as empty retail air, not as a slogan.
when: Use it when the image should feel like a unused future on worn tape. Do not use it as a crime night or as a hard neon-noir alley.
vs: Vaporwave is pastel, centered, and tape-soft. Neo-Noir is hard, rainy, and guilty.
Neon Practicals is the tube. Cross Process is a chemical hue shift.
Tech Noir still investigates. If the face is unfilled and the street is wet, you have left the mall.
examples_film: Drive supplies adjacent night grammar (pink-cyan practicals) but remains neo-noir in blocking. The look itself is more native to music video and internet stills than to a single film cycle.
Use Drive only as a cousin for hue, not as a crime template.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Neo-Noir : rain, hard key, raincoat. The tell is an unfilled cheek and wet asphalt.
Fix: flatten the contrast, center the frame, add marble or palms, and let VHS chroma bleed the edges.

faq.q: What is Vaporwave in film?
faq.a: A pastel look of pink-cyan wash, marble, palms, mall light, and VHS bleed. It nostalgizes a retail future that never arrived. It is not a crime lighting plot unless you force one.

faq.q: Vaporwave vs Neo-Noir
faq.a: Both may use cyan and magenta. Neo-noir keeps hard keys, rain, and isolation. Vaporwave keeps even fill, sculpture, and tape softness. Hue overlap is not the same look.

faq.q: When should I use Vaporwave?
faq.a: When the beat is unused-future nostalgia on consumer tape. Skip it for investigation, for hard rain, or for early-web horror (that is Weirdcore ).

faq.q: How do I prompt Vaporwave for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Vaporwave treatment of [Subject], pink-cyan gradient, marble and palms, VHS bleed, centered 35mm, mall fluorescent fill. Do not add a hard unfilled noir cheek.

title: Video Game
narrative: The world is playable. A character moves and the camera booms behind at a fixed height, or the map is seen at 45 degrees, or we look through a reticle.
Collectible space, ledges, and arenas matter. A HUD may sit in the glass.
It is not Pixel Art unless the level is also tiled. It is not FPV Drone (a real or simulated racing drone through a physical world).
It is not photoreal live action with a fake reticle slapped on. The camera must behave like a game camera.
how: Pick the logic: third-person follow (boom 2 to 3 meters, lag, collision), isometric 45-degree orthographic, or FPS. Keep the path readable.
Add a HUD only if the beat is play, not if it is a movie cover of a game. Motion: analog stick ease, not a film dolly's ease.
Prompt follow cam or isometric logic, HUD implied, space as a level.
when: Use it when space must feel playable. Do not use it as a skin on a normal coverage scene, and do not reduce it to chunky pixels unless the game is pixel-art.
vs: Video Game is engine-like camera logic. Pixel Art is sampling.
FPV Drone is a physical flying camera through real space. Animation may render a game, or not.
If the camera dollies like a film crew and there is no follow, iso, or FPS constraint, it is not this look.
examples_film: Free Guy (a life inside a game's follow-cam and HUD logic). Scott Pilgrim vs.
the World (fight space, UI, and level logic inside live action). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Pixel Art or a film Follow Shot shot with a reticle overlay. The tell is continuous film blocking, or tiles you did not want.
Fix: lock boom height or isometric angle, make the path a level, and let the camera collide or lag like an engine.

faq.q: What is Video Game in film?
faq.a: A look that borrows playable camera logic: follow cam, isometric, or FPS, with space as a level and often a HUD. The lens is constrained like an engine, not like a film crew.

faq.q: Video Game vs Pixel Art
faq.a: Pixel art is how the image is sampled. Video-game cinematography is how the camera is allowed to move through a playable space. A game look can be 3D and continuous. Pixel art cannot hide its tiles.

faq.q: When should I use Video Game?
faq.a: When the beat is play: a level, a follow, a HUD, a boss arena. Skip it for a normal coverage scene with a fake overlay, for drone FPV, or for pixel tiles that are not in the brief.

faq.q: How do I prompt Video Game for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Video-game camera on [Subject], follow cam or isometric logic, HUD implied, space as a level. Name boom height or the 45-degree view. Do not describe a film dolly by default.

title: Weirdcore
narrative: A face is cut by the frame edge. A caption sits in a default font.
JPEG blocks crawl. A toy in the dark is both funny and wrong.
Resolution is a weapon. The familiar (a bedroom, a mall, a smile) is encoded badly on purpose.
It is not Dreamcore . Dreamcore is soft, spatial, analog-liminal.
Weirdcore is digital-degraded, captioned, clipart-adjacent. It is not Altered State smear.
The warp is compression and crop, not a trip.
how: Crush the resolution. Allow JPEG artifacts, 240p, chromatic cheapness.
Crop faces wrong. On-camera flash or underexposed analog dark.
Optional captions. Palette: Windows-era interiors, flash skin, crushed blacks.
Prompt early-web dread, low-res sacred, a joke that is also a threat.
when: Use it when the familiar must look incorrectly encoded. Do not use it for a soft memory hall, for a psychedelic warp, or for polished vaporwave marble.
vs: Weirdcore is low-res, cropped, captioned threat. Dreamcore is a soft empty room.
Altered State smears perception. Vaporwave is pastel, marble, and tape-nostalgia without the joke-threat.
Stylistic Suck is amateur video as a film's voice. Weirdcore is specifically early-web incorrectness.
examples_film: Skinamarink (dark analog rooms, toys, faces withheld, internet-horror adjacent). Internet horror stills and early-web images supply the native grammar.
Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Dreamcore or Vaporwave : a soft hall, or a pink-cyan mall. The tell is continuous high-res pastel.
Fix: crush the file, crop wrong, add a cheap flash or a caption, and let the joke threaten.

faq.q: What is Weirdcore in film?
faq.a: A look that encodes the familiar badly: low resolution, wrong crops, captions, early-web artifacts, and a joke that is also a threat. The file is the fear.

faq.q: Weirdcore vs Dreamcore
faq.a: Dreamcore is analog-soft liminal space, a memory room. Weirdcore is digital-degraded and captioned. One withholds safety with empty architecture. The other withholds it with a bad encode.

faq.q: When should I use Weirdcore?
faq.a: When the familiar should look incorrectly rendered, as if an old file opened wrong. Skip it for soft nostalgia halls, for pastel marble, or for perception smear.

faq.q: How do I prompt Weirdcore for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Weirdcore image of [Subject], early-web dread, low-res sacred, wrong crop, JPEG artifacts, a joke that is also a threat. Do not polish into dreamcore softness.

title: Wuxia
narrative: The fight is a poem in a real (or studio-built) landscape. A body travels a wire path through Mist .
A Long Shot keeps honor readable as choreography, not as a blur of impacts. Silk and banners carry hue.
The camera cranes or holds wide so the land remains the other actor. It is the wrong tool for a grit street fight or a dusty gun standoff.
Hong Kong urban kung fu wants handheld wides and hits. Spaghetti Western wants hard sun and eyes.
Wuxia wants weather, fabric, and a path through air.
how: 35 spherical or anamorphic. 24mm to 40mm for wire wides, 50mm to 75mm to compress bamboo.
Mist or smoke as diffusion, not as a night-club haze. Crane, jib, or wire-rig the performer so the path has a rise and a float.
Slow the strike, not the walk. Palette: silk dyes, forest green, desert gold, color-coded armies if the story needs them.
Prompt misted bamboo, wire-fu weightlessness implied, silk color, heroic wides, Crouching Tiger air as weather, not as a slogan.
when: Use it when martial myth needs landscape and a weightless path. Do not use it for a bar brawl, a gun standoff, or a handheld hit sequence.
vs: Wuxia is mist, silk, wire, and Long Shot geography. Spaghetti Western is ochre, hard sun, and eye close-ups.
Mist is the atmosphere only. Long Shot is the size only.
A street kung-fu look is the opposite: wide, close, dirty, and weighted. Do not swap them.
examples_film: Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (bamboo canopy, rooftop paths, wire as flight). Hero (color-coded armies, desert and lake as moral spaces).
House of Flying Daggers (forest, silk, and a fight that is also a dance). Grammar, not frames to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a grit martial film or Spaghetti Western : sweat, ochre, and punches, or a noon standoff. The tell is no mist, no wire path, and a camera in the fighters' faces.
Fix: widen up, add mist, show the path through air, and let costume carry color.

faq.q: What is Wuxia in film?
faq.a: A martial-chivalry look: landscape wides, mist or silk weather, wire-assisted weightless movement, and color as costume rather than as a gelled threat. The fight is staged as myth, not as a street beating.

faq.q: Wuxia vs Spaghetti Western
faq.a: Both mythologize landscape. Wuxia uses mist, silk, and wire paths. Spaghetti western uses hard sun, dust, and telephoto eyes. Different weather, different combat, different close-up.

faq.q: When should I use Wuxia?
faq.a: When a martial beat needs land, weather, and a floating path. Skip it for gun standoffs, for urban handheld fights, or for horror gels.

faq.q: How do I prompt Wuxia for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Wuxia look on [Subject], misted bamboo, wire-fu weightlessness implied, silk color, long-shot landscape. Name the path through air. Do not ask for a dusty standoff or a street brawl.

title: 24mm Wide
narrative: This is the environmental portrait length. You can see the hands, the floor, and the doorway, and the face still belongs to a human rather than a mural.

Reportage interiors, street coverage, and walking masters live here because the room is a partner, not a special effect. It is the wrong tool when the space should attack the face, or when the face should erase the space.
A closer 14mm will balloon the near ground. An 85mm Portrait will melt the room into stacked color.
If the beat is most narrative talk with a little extra world, 35mm Moderate Wide is the quieter default.
how: Stand first: usually a few feet back, not on the nose. 24mm then includes a generous field with only moderate perspective stretch on a full-frame or Super 35 sensor.

Keep the camera closer to eye height unless rank is the point; a low 24mm will still heroic the figure because of the field, not because of a power slogan. Hands and foreground furniture will read large, so place them on purpose.
Prompt: 24mm wide on [Subject], environmental portrait, body in space, moderate stretch, reportage coverage.
when: Use it when a person plus their place must share the frame, neither winning: a soldier in a kitchen, a walker in a street. Do not use it to fake 14mm intrusion or 85mm isolation.
vs: 14mm Ultra-Wide from close exaggerates near-to-far size until the room attacks. 35mm Moderate Wide shows less world and less stretch, the usual storyteller step inward.
50mm Normal from the same stand crops the environment. Anamorphic is a squeeze system, not a wider 24mm.
examples_film: Children of Men often covers bodies in threatened rooms at a wide-normal that still lets geography read. The Hurt Locker does similar work in streets and interiors: person plus place, neither a poster.
Use that grammar of shared space, not a matching still.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is 14mm Ultra-Wide or 35mm Moderate Wide . The 14mm tell is a looming foreground and cartoon edges.
The 35mm tell is a tighter room with the environment demoted. Fix: stand a few feet back, hold full body or three-quarter plus readable architecture, keep stretch moderate.

faq.q: What is 24mm wide in film?
faq.a: It is a moderately wide lens that holds a person and a usable amount of their environment without extreme near-to-far exaggeration. Body and place share the frame.

faq.q: 24mm Wide vs 35mm Moderate Wide
faq.a: 24mm includes more architecture and a little more stretch. 35mm is the common narrative step tighter: still human, less room. 24mm is reportage space. 35mm is default coverage.

faq.q: When should I use 24mm wide?
faq.a: Use it when the beat is person plus place, neither winning. Skip it for close portraits and for ultra-wide intrusion.

faq.q: How do I prompt 24mm wide for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: 24mm wide on [Subject], environmental portrait, body in space, moderate stretch, reportage coverage. Name the room. Forbid fisheye bowing and telephoto falloff.

title: 35mm Moderate Wide
narrative: Most talking scenes want this field. You see the listener's shoulder, a lamp, a slice of wall, and a face that does not balloon.

The glass does a little editorial work (more place than a 50) without turning the room into a character the way 24mm and 14mm do. It is the wrong tool when the location must dominate, or when the person must become the only landscape.
Street masters and kitchen two-shots often belong at 24mm. Isolation close-ups belong at 85mm.
If you shoot every size on 35mm, the coverage matches, but you never change how space feels.
how: Stand at a conversational distance, roughly the same as a person talking across a table or a small room. On Super 35, 35mm sits near format-normal; on full frame it is a mild wide.
Either way the perspective is gentle if you do not crowd the nose. Keep verticals honest unless a tilt is the sentence.
Prompt: 35mm on [Subject], storyteller focal length, natural perspective with a little more world than 50.
when: Use it for most narrative coverage that should feel human but not telephoto: a two-shot at a table, a walk through a doorway. Do not use it as the only length in a film that needs space to change meaning.
vs: 24mm Wide shows more architecture and more stretch. 50mm Normal crops toward the conversation and editorialize less.
85mm Portrait from farther back isolates the face and stacks the background. 35mm is the middle storyteller, not a look.
examples_film: Moonlight often covers faces in rooms at a moderate wide-normal so Miami stays present without becoming a postcard. Manchester by the Sea does the same with New England interiors: people in places, neither squeezed nor stretched.
Grammar for default coverage, not a frame to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is 50mm Normal (too little room) or 24mm Wide (too much stretch). The tell is either a tight conversational crop with a melted wall, or a reportage wide with looming furniture.
Fix: conversational stand, face plus a true slice of place, mild perspective.

faq.q: What is 35mm moderate wide in film?
faq.a: It is the common narrative wide-normal: a little more world than a 50mm, without the stretch of a 24mm. Faces stay human and rooms stay readable.

faq.q: 35mm Moderate Wide vs 50mm Normal
faq.a: 35mm includes more of the room from the same stand. 50mm is tighter and less willing to show place. 35mm is default story coverage. 50mm is the glass that refuses to editorialize.

faq.q: When should I use 35mm moderate wide?
faq.a: Use it for most talk and coverage that needs face and room together. Skip it when the location should dominate or when the face should be the whole country.

faq.q: How do I prompt 35mm moderate wide for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: 35mm on [Subject], storyteller focal length, natural perspective with a little more world than 50. Name a slice of the room. Forbid 14mm distortion and 85mm isolation.

title: 50mm Normal
narrative: A 50mm is the length you pick when the sentence should sound like looking, not like a lens. Faces keep proportion.
Rooms neither rush forward nor crowd in. Conversations, over-the-shoulders, and plain singles live here because the audience is not asked to notice the optic.
It is the wrong tool when space itself must argue. A 24mm will make the room a partner.
An 85mm will make the person a landscape. From the same tripod, switching to 50mm only crops; if you wanted compression you still have to walk back, then use longer glass.
how: Stand first at a human talking distance. On a roughly 35mm-wide sensor, 50mm is a mild tele-normal; on full frame it is the classic still-camera normal.
Either way, keep the nodal point where a person would stand, and let the field fall out. Depth of field at 50mm is moderate unless you open very wide or get close.
Prompt: 50mm normal lens on [Subject], human-scale perspective, neither compressed nor stretched, conversational truth.
when: Use it when you do not want the glass to editorialize: a talk across a table, a single that should feel observed rather than styled. Do not use it to fake telephoto isolation or wide environmental stretch from a fixed stand.
vs: 35mm Moderate Wide shows a little more world from the same stand. 85mm Portrait requires a farther stand and starts to compress the background.
Spherical is the lens construction; a 50mm is usually spherical, but spherical is not a focal length. 24mm Wide from close is a different sentence about space.
examples_film: Classical coverage often parks the 50mm on singles and over-the-shoulders so the optic disappears and performance plus blocking carry the scene. Use that as grammar: conversational distance, honest proportion, no stacked city and no looming furniture.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is 35mm Moderate Wide labeled as normal, or 85mm Portrait because generators treat every face as a portrait length. The tell is extra room (35) or a washed, stacked background (85).
Fix: talking-distance stand, full-face proportion, background present but not crowding.

faq.q: What is 50mm normal in film?
faq.a: It is the conventional normal focal length: a field that neither stretches near objects nor compresses distant planes from a typical stand. Perspective still comes from where you put the camera.

faq.q: 50mm Normal vs 85mm Portrait
faq.a: 50mm at talking distance keeps the room honest and the face unstacked. 85mm from farther back enlarges the background, thins depth of field, and isolates. 50mm is conversation. 85mm is the face as landscape.

faq.q: When should I use 50mm normal?
faq.a: Use it when the optic should disappear: talk, witness, plain coverage. Skip it when space must stretch, stack, or isolate.

faq.q: How do I prompt 50mm normal for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: 50mm normal lens on [Subject], human-scale perspective, neither compressed nor stretched, conversational truth. Name a talking distance. Forbid ultra-wide stretch and telephoto stack.

title: 85mm Portrait
narrative: Walk back until an 85mm fills the frame with a face. Noses stop dominating.
Ears sit in proportion. The wall behind them comes forward as a soft plane rather than a readable room.
Isolation is the job: a person is the country, and everyone else is weather. It is the wrong tool for geography.

You cannot hold a kitchen two-shot honestly at 85mm in a small room because you cannot get far enough, and if you could, the space would flatten into wallpaper. If the beat is person plus place, go to 35mm Moderate Wide or 24mm Wide .
If the beat is surveillance from across a street, you wanted 135mm Telephoto .
how: Stand first, farther than conversation. Restore subject size with 85mm.

That distant viewpoint is what compresses facial features and enlarges background objects; the 85mm only chooses the crop. Open the aperture if you want rapid falloff, but shallow focus is a separate choice from the length.
Keep the camera at eye height unless you mean a power tilt. Prompt: 85mm portrait of [Subject], compressed background, rapid falloff, isolation, the face as the only country.
when: Use it when a person is the landscape: a close-up of thought, a romantic single, a face that should not share billing with the room. Do not use it for masters, group geography, or any beat that still needs architecture as a partner.
vs: 50mm Normal from closer keeps the room honest. 135mm Telephoto stacks even harder and feels like eavesdropping.
Shallow Focus can happen on many lengths; 85mm is a stand plus a crop, not a synonym for blur. Macro is close-focusing on a tiny object, not a portrait length.
examples_film: Her often isolates faces against a soft city so the person is the only country in the frame. Portrait cinema in general uses short telephotos this way: farther stand, larger face, background as a plane.
Borrow the distance and the isolation, not a still of Joaquin Phoenix.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is 50mm Normal or a wide close-up that balloons the nose. The tell is a large room still readable behind a close face, or a stretched forehead from standing too close with short glass.
Fix: walk back, 85mm, face large, background stacked and secondary.

faq.q: What is 85mm portrait in film?
faq.a: It is a short telephoto used from a farther stand so a face stays large while the background enlarges and loses importance. The person reads as the landscape.

faq.q: 85mm Portrait vs 50mm Normal
faq.a: 50mm at talking distance still shows a honest room. 85mm from farther back compresses that room into a plane and isolates the face. Same crop size, different stand, different space.

faq.q: When should I use 85mm portrait?
faq.a: Use it when the face is the scene and the room should not compete. Skip it for geography, two-shots in small rooms, and environmental portraits.

faq.q: How do I prompt 85mm portrait for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: 85mm portrait of [Subject], compressed background, rapid falloff, isolation, the face as the only country. Specify head-and-shoulders. Forbid wide stretch and readable architecture.

title: 135mm Telephoto
narrative: From across a street, a parking lot, or a sports field, 135mm restores a person to usable size and collapses the air between them and whatever sits behind. Cars, crowds, and buildings become a wall.
Approaches take forever. Isolation here is not portrait softness; it is surveillance distance.
It is the wrong tool inside a small room. You cannot get far enough, and if you force it the blocking dies.

It is also the wrong tool for a tender head-and-shoulders that should still feel like a conversation: that is 85mm Portrait . If the stack must be extreme, with heat shimmer and sniper intimacy, you wanted 200mm Long Telephoto .
how: Walk far away first. 135mm then crops that distant view tightly.

Compression is the distant viewpoint; the long lens only chooses how much of it to keep. Expect a thin depth of field even at moderate apertures, and expect atmospheric haze or heat if the throw is long enough.
A stick or beanbag beats handheld at this length. Prompt: 135mm telephoto on [Subject], stacked planes, eavesdropping compression, background crowding the figure.
when: Use it for surveillance, sports, or a stacked city: a figure watched from a rooftop, a runner against a wall of spectators. Do not use it for table coverage or any scene whose geography needs deep, receding space.
vs: 85mm Portrait is the nearer telephoto: isolation without the eavesdrop. 200mm Long Telephoto is farther and harder, with more shimmer and less escape in depth.
Telephoto Compression is the perspective effect itself, which 135mm often frames. Macro is close-up scale, the opposite throw.
examples_film: The Conversation uses long glass as listening: Harry is in the crowd and apart from it. Heat stacks Los Angeles so bodies and city occupy the same plane.
Those films treat distance as a moral fact. Borrow the throw and the stack, not a matching still.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is 85mm Portrait (too near, too kind) or a wide shot labeled telephoto. The tell is a readable receding street, or a close conversational background.
Fix: put the camera far away, stack the background against the body, keep the throw obvious.

faq.q: What is 135mm telephoto in film?
faq.a: It is a long lens used from a distant stand so depth planes stack and the background crowds the subject. The feeling is surveillance or sports distance, not a close conversation.

faq.q: 135mm Telephoto vs 85mm Portrait
faq.a: 85mm isolates a face from a portrait working distance. 135mm requires more throw, stacks the world harder, and reads as eavesdropping. 85mm is intimacy. 135mm is watching from away.

faq.q: When should I use 135mm telephoto?
faq.a: Use it for surveillance, sports, or a city that should press against a person. Skip it for small-room coverage and ordinary talk.

faq.q: How do I prompt 135mm telephoto for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: 135mm telephoto on [Subject], stacked planes, eavesdropping compression, background crowding the figure. Name the long throw. Forbid wide stretch and close-stand portraits.

title: 200mm Long Telephoto
narrative: At 200mm you are often so far that the air itself becomes part of the optic: heat, dust, and haze sit in layers. A walker seems not to approach.
A face can be in their pores while the desert, the compound, or the crowd is a flat wall glued to their shoulders. It is the wrong tool for any scene that must explain left and right in a room.

It is also the wrong tool if you only wanted portrait isolation; 85mm already does that without the shimmer and the unreachable camera. If the stack is a city street rather than a desert or a sniper line, 135mm Telephoto is usually enough.
how: Stand very far first, then restore size with 200mm. Support the camera; angular shake is huge at this length.
Focus is unforgiving. Expect a thin slice of sharpness and, outdoors, visible atmospheric disturbance along the path.

Do not confuse this with digital zoom from a 50mm stand: that crop has no compression because you never moved. Prompt: 200mm long lens on [Subject], extreme compression, heat shimmer, isolated from a distance, sniper intimacy.
when: Use it when you must be far away and still in their pores: a desert rider, a compound watch, a face across a canyon of air. Do not use it for dialogue coverage or for a portrait you could have made at 85mm.
vs: 135mm Telephoto is the nearer long lens, stacked but less extreme. Telephoto Compression names the viewpoint effect 200mm often shows.
85mm Portrait is intimacy from a portrait stand, not this throw. Macro is the opposite: inches, not hundreds of meters.
examples_film: Lawrence of Arabia uses heat telephotos so distant riders take an age to arrive through shimmer. Zero Dark Thirty uses long glass as watcher's distance on compounds and streets.
Grammar of throw and air, not a poster of a silhouette.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is 135mm Telephoto or a cropped 50mm labeled 200mm. The tell is too much remaining depth, or no atmospheric stack.
Fix: put real distance between camera and subject, let planes glue together, allow haze or heat if outdoors.

faq.q: What is 200mm long telephoto in film?
faq.a: It is an extreme long lens used from a very distant stand. Planes stack until there is almost no escape in depth, and air or heat often sits in the image.

faq.q: 200mm Long Telephoto vs 135mm Telephoto
faq.a: Both stack space from far away. 200mm needs more throw, compresses harder, and more often shows heat shimmer or sniper distance. 135mm is stacked city or sports. 200mm is the farther wall.

faq.q: When should I use 200mm long telephoto?
faq.a: Use it for desert approaches, compound surveillance, or any beat that must stay far and still read pores. Skip it for rooms, talk, and ordinary portraits.

faq.q: How do I prompt 200mm long telephoto for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: 200mm long lens on [Subject], extreme compression, heat shimmer, isolated from a distance, sniper intimacy. State the huge throw. Forbid wide fields and close-stand faces.

title: Anamorphic
narrative: The frame can hold a face and a landscape in the same breath because the desqueezed field is wide while the taking lens may still be a moderate focal length. Highlights streak sideways.
Out-of-focus lamps become ovals. The optic announces a movie without needing black bars glued onto a spherical image.
39:1. Cropping a Spherical 50mm and adding letterbox is an aspect ratio, not this glass.
It is also the wrong tool if you need clinical edges and round bokeh. Not every anamorphic lens flares the same way; do not treat Anamorphic Flare as automatic.
how: 8x) or recreate specific optical traits with restraint. Keep desqueezed geometry correct: circles in the world must not stay squeezed in the final image.
Focus breathing and a thinner vertical taking field are common. Oval bokeh comes from the cylindrical elements, not from a filter sticker.
Prompt: Anamorphic 2x on [Subject], oval bokeh, horizontal flares, widescreen squeeze character.
when: Use it when the frame should announce itself as widescreen glass: a night interior with oval lamps, a face in a wide city. Do not use it as a synonym for letterbox, and do not sprinkle blue streaks on every spherical shot.
vs: Spherical has round bokeh and rectilinear edges with no squeeze. Anamorphic Flare is one artifact some anamorphic lenses produce, not the whole system.
Vintage Cine Glass can be spherical or anamorphic; vintage is coatings and contrast, not the squeeze. Black bars on a 16:9 file are not this technique.
examples_film: Blade Runner uses anamorphic night interiors and city imagery as a widescreen optical fact. Inception 's live-action photography is largely anamorphic widescreen.
La La Land and The Batman lean on oval highlights and directional flares as part of that glass. Borrow the squeeze behavior, not a copyrighted still.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Spherical footage with black bars, or a flare overlay without oval highlights. The tell is round lamps, no squeeze character, and a 16:9 image with mats.
Fix: oval bokeh, horizontal highlight streaks, desqueezed widescreen geometry. A wide aspect ratio alone is not anamorphic.

faq.q: What is anamorphic in film?
faq.a: It is a lens system that squeezes one dimension at capture and expands it for viewing. Many such lenses add oval bokeh and directional flares. Widescreen shape by itself is not anamorphic.

faq.q: Anamorphic vs Spherical
faq.a: Spherical lenses do not squeeze; bokeh is typically round and edges stay rectilinear. Anamorphic lenses squeeze, then desqueeze, and often ovalize highlights. Letterboxing a spherical image does not convert it.

faq.q: When should I use anamorphic?
faq.a: Use it when you want the specific optical behavior of squeeze glass: oval lamps, horizontal flares, a wide field from a moderate taking length. Skip it if you only wanted black bars.

faq.q: How do I prompt anamorphic for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Anamorphic 2x on [Subject], oval bokeh, horizontal flares, widescreen squeeze character. Demand desqueezed geometry. Forbid round bokeh and simple letterbox.

title: Telephoto Compression
narrative: Walk away until a far building and a near figure occupy similar size, then crop with 135mm or 200mm. Escape routes in depth disappear.
An approaching rider takes an age. A fallen body and a car can look glued together.
The air gets crowded even when the location is huge. It is the wrong tool when space should recede.
From close with wide glass, near objects balloon and far walls drop away, the opposite sentence. Do not zoom in from a fixed tripod and call it compression: that is only a crop.
Stand first, then glass.
how: Move farther away until the relative sizes of planes collapse, then choose a long focal length to restore the subject's size in the frame. Keep atmospheric haze, foreground overlaps, and focus consistent with that distance.

A 200mm from 50 meters compresses; a 200mm crop of a 35mm file shot from 3 meters does not. Prompt: Telephoto compression stacking [Subject] against a wall of background, distances collapsed, crowded air, no escape in depth.
when: Use it when the city, army, or terrain should sit right on their back: a walker who cannot outrun the buildings. Do not use it as a synonym for any long lens, and do not claim compression from a close stand.
vs: 200mm Long Telephoto and 135mm Telephoto are lengths that often frame this viewpoint. Compression is the standpoint, not the millimeter number.
85mm Portrait starts the stack but still feels like a portrait distance. 14mm Ultra-Wide from close is the anti-compression: exaggerated size differences.
examples_film: Lawrence of Arabia lets Sherif Ali approach through desert shimmer as a study in collapsed distance. Payback glues a fallen figure and a car in depth.
Heat and Chungking Express stack cities so people have no air behind them. Grammar of viewpoint, not a copied composition.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a long-lens label on a close-stand shot, or a wide that still shows receding space. The tell is large size differences between near and far, or a cropped 35mm perspective.
Fix: walk away, long glass, planes of similar apparent size, crowded air.

faq.q: What is telephoto compression in film?
faq.a: It is the flattening of size differences between depth planes caused by a distant camera position. A long lens then tightly frames that view. The lens alone, from a fixed stand, does not change perspective.

faq.q: Telephoto Compression vs 200mm Long Telephoto
faq.a: 200mm is a focal length. Compression is what a distant stand does to planes, often framed with 135mm or 200mm. You can shoot 200mm from too close and get no stack. You can compress with other long lengths if you walk far enough.

faq.q: When should I use telephoto compression?
faq.a: Use it when a crowd, city, or landscape should press against a person, or when an approach should seem never to arrive. Skip it when space must recede.

faq.q: How do I prompt telephoto compression for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Telephoto compression stacking [Subject] against a wall of background, distances collapsed, crowded air, no escape in depth. Demand a far camera. Forbid wide close-stand perspective.

title: Fisheye
narrative: Put a face in the middle and the room circles them. Put them off-center and their skull stretches along the barrel.
The mapping can be circular (a round image in a black frame) or diagonal (the circle fills the rectangle). Either way, the mind of the shot is warped, or the space is a dome.
It is the wrong tool when you wanted extreme width with straight walls. That is a rectilinear 14mm Ultra-Wide .
Random wobbly architecture is a model failure, not fisheye projection. If the beat is only a mildly wide room, 24mm Wide already does it without the wrap.
how: Choose circular or full-frame fisheye and stage faces near the center unless edge stretching is deliberate. Keep the distortion systematic: lines bow around a stable center, they do not ripple.
A zenith or dome shot will map the room as a globe. Prompt: Fisheye on [Subject], circular or extreme barrel distortion, a world wrapping around a face, subjective unreality.
when: Use it when the mind is warped, or the space is a dome: a palace that should feel wrong, a subjective spiral, a helmet-cam joke. Do not use it as a synonym for 14mm, and do not apply random warping.
vs: 14mm Ultra-Wide is rectilinear: huge field, straight-ish lines, stretch from a close stand. Fisheye is curvilinear by design.
24mm Wide is moderate and polite. Kaleidoscope multiplies fragments; fisheye is one continuous wrap.
examples_film: The Favourite bends palace interiors under conspicuously wide, curvilinear views. Poor Things uses highly distorted wide-angle views so the world stays unfamiliar.
A Clockwork Orange and Being John Malkovich have used extreme wide wrap as subjective pressure. Grammar of bowing space, not a filter preset.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is 14mm Ultra-Wide with extra warp, or a wavy hallucination. The tell is straight walls that should bow, or unstable rippling.
Fix: systematic barrel around a clear center, horizon curved, face protected unless you mean the stretch.

faq.q: What is fisheye in film?
faq.a: It is a curvilinear ultra-wide projection that bends straight lines away from the center. The field wraps around the lens instead of drawing a rectilinear box.

faq.q: Fisheye vs 14mm Ultra-Wide
faq.a: A 14mm rectilinear ultra-wide keeps lines mostly straight and exaggerates size from a close stand. A fisheye bows those lines on purpose. Width is not the same as wrap.

faq.q: When should I use fisheye?
faq.a: Use it when unreality, comedy, or a dome of space is the point. Skip it for ordinary wides and for rectilinear 14mm intrusion.

faq.q: How do I prompt fisheye for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Fisheye on [Subject], circular or extreme barrel distortion, a world wrapping around a face, subjective unreality. Specify circular versus full-frame fill. Forbid random wobble and rectilinear 14mm.

title: Macro
narrative: The plot becomes a centimeter. A pill, a watch gear, a drop, a pupil: the object is no longer an insert in a room, it is the room.
Depth of field collapses to a millimeter, so a breath or a rack is a traverse across a landscape of pores. It is the wrong tool when you only wanted a tight face.

An Extreme Close-Up of an eye can be a long lens from a foot away; that is a crop, not macro scale. A normal close-up enlarged in post does not automatically have convincing macro texture or depth of field.
If you need to travel through a glass or a machine, that is a Probe Lens .
how: Use a macro lens or close-focus setup, stabilize the object, and light for surface texture (small hard sources show relief; wrap shows translucency). Anticipate shallow depth of field and tiny focus changes.
Working distance is short; watch your own shadow. Magnification is image size over object size, not the shot-size name.
Prompt: Macro lens on a detail of [Subject], insects of texture, an eye, a watch, a drop of rain, a world in a centimeter.
when: Use it when the plot is microscopic: a ritual of pills, a bug, a lock mechanism. Do not use it as a synonym for close-up, and do not blow up a normal portrait and call it macro.
vs: Extreme Close-Up is a framing size; it may or may not use macro optics. Insert Shot is a story object in the cut, any size.
Probe Lens is a long barrel that can enter tiny spaces with a wide-ish view. Magnification is the scale number; macro is one optical way to get it.
examples_film: Requiem for a Dream repeats extreme-detail images so rituals compress into sensory fragments. Amélie turns ordinary objects into tactile small pleasures.
Microcosmos treats insects as full-scale drama. Grammar of close-focus scale, not a copied frame of a pupil.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is an Extreme Close-Up made with a portrait lens, or a zoomed crop. The tell is normal skin-pore size with deep-ish focus, or a whole face labeled macro.
Fix: small object filling the sensor, true close-focus falloff, texture lit as terrain.

faq.q: What is macro in film?
faq.a: It is close-focusing photography that reproduces a small object at high scale, often around life-size on the sensor. Texture and tiny depth of field become the image.

faq.q: Macro vs Extreme Close-Up
faq.a: An extreme close-up is a crop of a feature, possible with a long lens from a foot away. Macro is an optical scale: a small object occupies the frame at high magnification with true close-focus depth of field.

faq.q: When should I use macro?
faq.a: Use it when a tiny object or surface is the scene. Skip it for ordinary portraits and for inserts that are merely tight, not close-focus.

faq.q: How do I prompt macro for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Macro lens on a detail of [Subject], a world in a centimeter, razor-thin focus, surface texture. Name the object. Forbid ordinary close-up and probe-through-a-tunnel unless you want those.

title: Magnification
narrative: Scale is lost on purpose. A tick, a spark, a cell of fabric becomes geography.
Powers of Ten is a ladder of magnification: each step changes what counts as a place. Going closer than a close-up is the beat, but closer optically, not only by cropping a 4K face.
It is the wrong tool when you meant a Close-Up of an actor from a meter away. That face may fill the frame at low magnification.
It is also the wrong tool if the path through a tiny space is the point: Probe Lens delivers that path. Macro is the usual optic that reaches 1:1; magnification is the measurement you are after.
how: Decide the reproduction ratio (1:2, 1:1, 2:1) and pick optics that can hold it: macro, bellows, probe, or microscope. Light for the new scale; apparent motion and camera shake scale up with magnification.
Depth of field collapses. Do not confuse digital punch-in with optical magnification: extra pixels are not extra scale.
Prompt: Extreme magnification of [Subject], a world inside a centimeter, scale lost on purpose.
when: Use it when you must go closer than a close-up in true scale: a world inside a centimeter. Do not use it as a synonym for a tight portrait or a cropped still.
vs: Macro is close-focusing optics that commonly reach these ratios. Probe Lens adds a barrel that can enter the small world.
Extreme Close-Up is a framing of a feature, which may be low magnification. Magnification is the scale, not the cutaway name Insert Shot .
examples_film: Microcosmos treats insect scale as full drama, true high magnification. Powers of Ten makes magnification itself the structure, stepping in and out of orders of size.
Use those as grammar for scale, not as frames to duplicate.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is an Extreme Close-Up or a punched-in Close-Up . The tell is a whole eye from portrait distance with moderate depth of field.
Fix: object scale on the sensor near life-size or greater, razor focus, centimeter geography.

faq.q: What is magnification in film?
faq.a: It is the ratio of image size on the sensor to the object's real size. High magnification fills the frame with a tiny piece of the world. Shot-size names like close-up do not guarantee that ratio.

faq.q: Magnification vs Macro
faq.a: Macro is a class of close-focusing lens, often able to reach 1:1. Magnification is the number you get. A probe or a microscope can magnify too. A portrait close-up of a face is usually low magnification.

faq.q: When should I use magnification?
faq.a: Use it when true scale must collapse to a centimeter or less. Skip it when you only needed a tight crop of a person.

faq.q: How do I prompt magnification for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Extreme magnification of [Subject], a world inside a centimeter, scale lost on purpose. Name the object and, if possible, 1:1. Forbid ordinary close-ups and simple punch-ins.

title: Probe Lens
narrative: The camera body stays outside. The tube goes where a camera cannot: through ice in a drink, between gears, across a tabletop forest, into a bottle.

The view is often wide at the tip, so a drop of liquid becomes a lake and a crumb becomes a boulder, while the move can travel through that world. It is the wrong tool when a standard Macro from outside already sees the surface you need.
It is also the wrong tool for a face portrait; the look is proximity through a hole, not an 85mm single. If you only wanted a 14mm in a normal room, you wanted 14mm Ultra-Wide , not a probe.
how: Mount the probe, protect the barrel, and plan a path the tip can physically travel. Light from outside the tiny space or fiber the interior; the front element is close to the subject and will see your flags if you are careless.
Depth of field is still small despite the typical slow stop, because you are close. Stabilize the move; inches are miles.
Prompt: Probe-lens view of [Subject], tiny wide lens on a stick, impossible proximity through glass, food, or machinery, miniature world.
when: Use it to go where a camera body cannot: through a drink, into a watch, across a plated meal as if it were terrain. Do not use it as a synonym for macro on a tabletop you could shoot from above.
vs: Macro photographs a small object from outside at high scale. A probe enters the space.
14mm Ultra-Wide is a wide field from a normal camera body. Magnification is the scale; the probe is a delivery system that also tends to be wide at the tip.
examples_film: Commercial food and product work uses probes constantly so a camera can travel through bubbles and garnish. The Hobbit's miniature-language cousins (and similar tabletop/miniature photography) rely on tiny viewpoints inside constructed worlds.
Treat those as grammar for impossible proximity, not as a still to copy.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Macro from outside, or a 14mm in a full-size room. The tell is a tabletop still with the camera clearly outside, or a normal interior wide.
Fix: viewpoint from inside a small space, barrel-path move, wide-at-the-tip scale.

faq.q: What is a probe lens in film?
faq.a: It is a long, narrow close-focus optic whose tiny front element can enter small spaces. You get extreme proximity and, often, a wide view from inside an object or miniature set.

faq.q: Probe Lens vs Macro
faq.a: Macro is close-focus from outside: a lens aimed at a small object. A probe is a barrel that can pass through that object or between objects, with the camera body remaining outside the tiny space.

faq.q: When should I use a probe lens?
faq.a: Use it when the shot must travel through a drink, a machine, food, or a miniature gap a camera body cannot enter. Skip it if a normal macro from outside already sees the surface.

faq.q: How do I prompt a probe lens for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Probe-lens view of [Subject], tiny wide lens on a stick, impossible proximity through glass, food, or machinery, miniature world. Name the path through the space. Forbid ordinary portraits and overhead macros.

title: Spherical
narrative: This is default modern capture. You pick a focal length, you stand somewhere, and the optic does not ovalize lamps or streak headlights into bars.
Sharpness and control are easier to specify because you are not also managing squeeze, desqueeze, and cylindrical artifacts. It is the wrong tool only when those artifacts are the point.
If the beat needs oval highlights and horizontal flares, you wanted Anamorphic . 39:1 still exists: you crop or use a large sensor.
That is an aspect ratio on spherical glass, not a conversion.
how: Choose a spherical prime or zoom and a stand. Perspective still comes from camera position; 24mm spherical is not 85mm spherical.
Keep the iris in mind if bokeh shape matters: a round iris yields round highlights; a many-bladed iris yields a polygon. No desqueeze in post.
Prompt: Spherical prime on [Subject], round bokeh, rectilinear edges, clean modern capture, no anamorphic streak.
when: Use it when you want control and sharpness over squeeze romance: most coverage, VFX plates, anything that must stitch or track cleanly. Do not label spherical footage anamorphic because you added black bars.
vs: Anamorphic squeezes and often ovalizes. 50mm Normal is a focal length you will often shoot spherical.
Vintage Cine Glass may be spherical glass with older coatings; vintage is not a squeeze. Fisheye is curvilinear spherical or a dedicated projection, still not anamorphic.
examples_film: Most modern digital cinema is spherical unless the production states otherwise. Use that as a reminder: round lamps, no horizontal streak from the taking lens, geometry that matches a prime's field.
The look is the stand and the length, not a flare pack.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Anamorphic stickers on a round-bokeh image. The tell is letterbox plus circular lamps plus random streaks.
Fix: round bokeh, no squeeze, rectilinear edges, and a named spherical focal length.

faq.q: What is spherical in film?
faq.a: Spherical lenses capture an unsqueezed image with rotationally symmetric optics. Highlights through a round iris stay round, and there is no anamorphic desqueeze.

faq.q: Spherical vs Anamorphic
faq.a: Spherical: no squeeze, typically round bokeh, rectilinear field. Anamorphic: squeeze at capture, oval bokeh, often directional flares. Cropping spherical footage to widescreen does not make it anamorphic.

faq.q: When should I use spherical?
faq.a: Use it as default glass when you need control, sharpness, or clean plates. Skip it only when the squeeze artifacts themselves are the sentence.

faq.q: How do I prompt spherical for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Spherical prime on [Subject], round bokeh, rectilinear edges, clean modern capture, no anamorphic streak. Add a real focal length. Forbid oval bokeh and horizontal flares.

title: Split Diopter
narrative: A telephone in the foreground and a doorway across the room can both be tack-sharp, with a narrow blur band where the half-lens ends. The construction is often hidden on a door edge, a lamp, or a dark seam.
The coexistence is the sentence: a face and a distant threat are equally true at once. It is the wrong tool when a small aperture and careful staging would hold both planes without a seam.
That is Deep Focus . It is also the wrong tool if you meant to throw attention from one plane to the other over time: that is Rack Focus .
Do not describe this as a split-screen or a ghost overlay.
how: Mount a split-field diopter in front of the taking lens so half the field is a close-up filter. Focus the naked side on the far subject; the diopter side will bring a near object into focus.
Hide the boundary against a vertical edge or a soft region. A two-focus composite can recreate the look with more control.
Prompt: One continuous room: a near object on the left tack-sharp and [Subject] far on the right also tack-sharp, a narrow blur band between them. Not a split-screen, not a ghost overlay.
when: Use it when two distances must both be true at once: a listener and a far figure, a glass and a door. Do not use it as a substitute for deep focus, and do not split the frame into two movies.
vs: Deep Focus holds near and far by stopping down and staging, with no diopter seam. Rack Focus changes which plane is sharp over time.
Split Screen cuts the frame into separate images. A split diopter is one take, two focus regions, a possible tell at the join.
examples_film: Blow Out holds near listening equipment or faces with distant action in the same composition. Jaws keeps near and far figures simultaneously sharp in selected setups.
The Conversation and Mission: Impossible have used the same charged coexistence. Grammar of two distances at once, not a copied still.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Deep Focus (no seam, everything held by aperture) or Split Screen (two images). The tell is a hard vertical cut, a double-exposed ghost, or uniform focus with no join.
Fix: two distance zones, both sharp, a narrow optical blur band, one continuous space.

faq.q: What is a split diopter in film?
faq.a: It is a partial close-up lens that lets one part of the frame focus very near while another part stays focused far away. The join often shows as a thin blur band.

faq.q: Split Diopter vs Deep Focus
faq.a: Deep focus uses a small aperture and staging so a single focus field covers near and far. A split diopter creates two different focus regions with an optical join. It is not two focal lengths and not a split-screen.

faq.q: When should I use a split diopter?
faq.a: Use it when a near object and a far figure must both be sharp at once and ordinary depth of field cannot hold them. Skip it if deep focus or a rack would tell the truth better.

faq.q: How do I prompt a split diopter for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write one continuous room with a near object and a far subject both tack-sharp and a narrow blur band between them. Forbid split-screen, ghost overlay, and ordinary deep focus.

title: Tilt-Shift
narrative: Tilt is not a blur sticker. The Scheimpflug relation puts a slice of the world in focus along a plane that is no longer parallel to the sensor: a street of rowers, a crowd, a tabletop of people who suddenly read as toys.
Shift is a different job: it slides the image to keep verticals parallel or to look around a corner without rotating the camera. It is the wrong tool when you only wanted a face isolated from a wall.
That is Shallow Focus on a normal plane. It is also the wrong tool if the miniature effect has no high viewpoint and no consistent focus band.
A horizontal blur strip that ignores perspective is a post fake, not this optic.
how: Tilt the lens so the focus plane cuts through the subject as a thin band or a wedge. A high angle helps the diorama reading because we look down on models.
Match blur to depth; as perspective changes, the band should follow the plane, not a 2D stripe. Shift independently if you need to correct converging buildings.
Prompt: A real-scale city or citadel with [Subject] human-sized. A thin band of focus across the subject, foreground and far ground softly blurred, no hard seam across the frame.
when: Use it to make a city a model, or to slice focus through a crowd on a tilted plane. Do not use it as a synonym for shallow portrait focus, and do not lay a blur bar across a flat image.
vs: Shallow Focus keeps the focus plane parallel to the sensor and isolates by distance. Tilt rotates that plane.
Macro is close-up scale, not a diorama of a city. Bird's-Eye View can supply the high viewpoint the miniature reading often needs, but a bird's-eye without a tilted focus plane is just a map.
examples_film: The Social Network 's Henley rowing sequence gives real-scale action a miniature-like appearance through a thin, high, diorama focus. Miniature-city treatments in other films follow the same grammar: high view, shallow band, motion that reads like a toy.
Borrow the plane, not a still of the race.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Shallow Focus on a face, or a post miniature with a 2D blur strip. The tell is a portrait with creamy background, or a seam that ignores buildings' depth.
Fix: high view, human-sized figures, focus as a plane through the scene, blur that follows depth.

faq.q: What is tilt-shift in film?
faq.a: Tilt rotates the plane of focus relative to the sensor. Shift slides the lens to change perspective without tilting the camera. Together they can isolate a band of sharpness or make real scenes read as models.

faq.q: Tilt-Shift vs Shallow Focus
faq.a: Shallow focus keeps the focus plane parallel to the sensor and falls off with distance. Tilt-shift can put a wedge or band of focus through a scene, including a high diorama view of a city. Blur shape is the difference.

faq.q: When should I use tilt-shift?
faq.a: Use it to slice focus through a crowd or to turn real-scale action into a model. Skip it for ordinary portraits that only need a fast 85mm.

faq.q: How do I prompt tilt-shift for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write that the subject is human-sized in a real city, with a thin band of focus and no hard seam. Add a high viewpoint for the diorama. Forbid a flat blur stripe and ordinary portrait bokeh.

title: 14mm Ultra-Wide
narrative: Stand an arm's length from a person and a 14mm still holds the ceiling, the corridor, and the street behind them. Near masses swell.
Far walls drop away. The figure is inside a space that will not stay polite, which is why the same glass can feel intimate and confrontational at once.
It is the wrong tool for a flattering head-and-shoulders. Edge stretch cartoons ears and cheeks unless the face stays near the optical axis.
If you only wanted a body plus a readable room without heroic geometry, step back and use 24mm Wide . If the walls must bow, that is Fisheye , not a rectilinear 14mm.
how: Stand first, then choose glass. Park the nodal point close enough that a hand, a table, or a face owns scale, then let 14mm include the rest.

Rectilinear 14mm keeps straight lines straighter than a fisheye; remaining stretch is perspective from that close viewpoint. Keep faces off the extreme frame edges unless further stretching is intended.
Architecture will fan from the lens axis. Prompt: 14mm ultra-wide on [Subject], exaggerated perspective, looming foreground, stretched architecture, slight heroic distortion.
when: Use it when the audience must sit inside a space that is too big or too close: a face in a hotel lobby that still owns the ceiling. Do not use 14mm as a default portrait lens, or as a sticker that means wide.
vs: 24mm Wide is the next stop: person plus place without this much ballooning. Fisheye bends those straight lines on purpose.
50mm Normal from the same close stand still crops the room out; 14mm is inclusion plus exaggeration. Forced Perspective is a staging trick along the axis; 14mm is an optical field from a close stand.
examples_film: The Revenant often works this close in weather so bodies and trees share one aggressive space. Birdman keeps wide glass in tight interiors so rooms never let the actors go.
Fallen Angels films faces against expanded urban night. Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas uses close wide proximity as subjective unease.
Borrow the stand and the field, not a still.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is Fisheye (bowed walls) or a distant 24mm Wide labeled 14mm. The tell is either curvilinear bowing or a calm environmental portrait with no looming foreground.
Fix: move close, keep lines mostly straight, let the near object own scale. Wide angle does not automatically distort a face from every distance; viewpoint is the dominant variable.

faq.q: What is 14mm ultra-wide in film?
faq.a: It is a very short rectilinear focal length used from a close stand so the field is huge and near objects dwarf far ones. The close camera position, not the 14mm label alone, creates that exaggeration.

faq.q: 14mm Ultra-Wide vs 24mm Wide
faq.a: 14mm from close makes foregrounds loom and rooms recede hard. 24mm still holds person plus place, but the stretch is moderate and faces survive better away from center. If the beat is reportage rather than intrusion, use 24mm.

faq.q: When should I use 14mm ultra-wide?
faq.a: Use it when a face or object must stay close while the surrounding world remains intrusive. Skip it for ordinary portraits, and skip it if you actually want fisheye bowing.

faq.q: How do I prompt 14mm ultra-wide for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: 14mm ultra-wide on [Subject], exaggerated perspective, looming foreground, stretched architecture, slight heroic distortion. Name the close stand. Forbid barrel distortion unless you want fisheye.

title: Vintage Cine Glass
narrative: Put a face on Cooke, K35, or similar older glass and the image rolls off instead of biting. Highlights bloom a little.
Contrast sits down. Backgrounds can swirl or breathe at the edges.
Memory, period, or beauty over resolution is the job of the optic, before anyone touches the timeline. It is the wrong tool when you need hard edges for VFX or a documentary fact.

It is also the wrong tool if you only wanted a faded grade on modern glass: that is Filmic Faded or a Vintage treatment, not this lens. Halation can be stock or a filter; vintage cine may contribute similar bloom, but the swirl and the contrast live in the glass.
how: Choose actual vintage or vintage-inspired cine primes and shoot them wide enough to show the aberrations. Do not stop down until they behave like modern glass if those aberrations are the point.
Keep skin highlights just hot enough to halate. Separate this from anamorphic squeeze: many vintage cine lenses are Spherical .
Prompt: Vintage cine glass on [Subject], lower contrast, gentle halation, swirling edges, Cooke or K35 character, not clinical sharpness.
when: Use it for memory, period, or a face that should not look like a catalog. Do not use it as a synonym for a faded LUT on a modern zoom.
vs: Anamorphic is a squeeze system; some vintage glass is anamorphic, most of this entry is about spherical old coatings. Halation is highlight bloom, one trait.
Filmic Faded is a print-emulation grade. Vintage is a whole period treatment.
Vintage cine is the taking lens.
examples_film: The Master and Phantom Thread are often cited for older or character glass on faces: lower bite, gentle bloom, a refusal of clinical digital edges. Use that as grammar for optic character, not as a still to match pixel for pixel.
mistakes: The usual wrong cousin is a Filmic Faded grade or a Vintage dye fade on sharp modern glass. The tell is crunchy edges with a brown LUT, or grain with no optical swirl or halation.
Fix: lower contrast in the taking image, gentle highlight bloom, edge character from the lens.

faq.q: What is vintage cine glass in film?
faq.a: It is older motion-picture lenses with coatings and aberrations that lower contrast, bloom highlights, and sometimes swirl the edges. The character is optical, not only a grade.

faq.q: Vintage Cine Glass vs Filmic Faded
faq.a: Filmic faded is a print-emulation grade: lifted blacks, rolled highlights. Vintage cine is the lens: coatings, swirl, optical bloom. You can have one without the other.

faq.q: When should I use vintage cine glass?
faq.a: Use it when the taking optic should be gentler than modern primes: memory, period, a face that should not look clinical. Skip it for hard VFX plates.

faq.q: How do I prompt vintage cine glass for AI image or video?
faq.a: Write: Vintage cine glass on [Subject], lower contrast, gentle halation, swirling edges, Cooke or K35 character, not clinical sharpness. Forbid LUT-only fade and anamorphic squeeze unless you want those too.
